docs.title: Configure auto mode
docs.text:
Tell the auto mode classifier which repos, buckets, and domains your organization trusts. Set environment context, override the default block and allow rules, and inspect your effective config with the auto-mode CLI subcommands.

Auto mode lets Claude Code run without routine permission prompts by routing tool calls through a classifier that blocks anything irreversible, destructive, or aimed outside your environment. Deny and explicit ask rules are evaluated before the classifier and still block or prompt. Use the autoMode settings block to tell that classifier which repos, buckets, and domains your organization trusts, so it stops blocking routine internal operations.

[!NOTE]

This page is the configuration reference. Turning auto mode on and off is covered on the Permission modes page:

  • Switch to auto mode mid-session, or back out of it: see Switch permission modes
  • Start a session in auto mode: see Start in a different permission mode

Auto mode is available to all users on every provider, including the Anthropic API, Claude Platform on AWS, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, and signed-in Claude apps gateway sessions. If Claude Code reports auto mode as unavailable for your account, check the full requirements, which also cover the supported models and the organization-level control on Team and Enterprise plans.

By default, the classifier trusts only the working directory and the current repo's configured remotes. Actions like pushing to your company's source-control org or writing to a team cloud bucket are blocked until you add them to autoMode.environment.

This page covers how to:

  • Add a human checkpoint for pushes and pull requests with permissions.ask
  • Define trusted infrastructure with autoMode.environment
  • Generate environment entries with /auto-mode-setup
  • Review denials so you know what to add next

docs.title: Common boundaries
docs.text:
Auto mode allows pushes to any branch of the repository you're working in, including the default branch, and pull request creation by default. A non-default branch whose name marks it as a deploy or publication target, such as production, release, or gh-pages, isn't covered by that default: the classifier judges a push there on its own terms, including as a production deploy. The push's content is also still checked, so a force push, a secret entering the commit, or a change that would send secrets outside the repository when CI or a deploy pipeline runs it stays blocked.

If you want a human checkpoint before Claude's push and pull request commands, add permission rules: the recipes below keep auto mode on for everything else.

docs.title: Add a human checkpoint
docs.text:
The most direct mechanism is permissions.ask. Content-scoped ask rules like the ones below are evaluated before the classifier and always force a permission prompt, even in auto mode, because an explicit ask rule is your stated intent to be prompted for that action. Add the rules in your settings:

```json theme={null} { "permissions": { "ask": [ "Bash(git push *)", "Bash(gh pr create *)" ] } } 

These rules match commands that begin with `git push` or `gh pr create`. A push Claude writes another way, such as `git -C <dir> push` or `git -c <key>=<value> push`, [doesn't match the rule](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions.md#bash-rule-limits), so it isn't checkpointed. For a checkpoint that inspects the full command text, add a [PreToolUse hook](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks.md#pretooluse).

Pick the mechanism that matches how firm the boundary needs to be:

| Boundary | Mechanism | Behavior in auto mode |
| :- | :- | :- |
| Prompt before the action | `permissions.ask` | Always prompts for a command that matches a content-scoped rule like the recipe above. The classifier cannot auto-approve a matching action. |
| Never run the action | `permissions.deny` | Blocks before the classifier is consulted. Neither the classifier nor user intent can override it. |
| One-off boundary for this session | State it in conversation, like "don't push until I review" | The classifier blocks matching actions, but the boundary can be lost if [context compaction](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/costs.md#reduce-token-usage) removes the message that stated it. Use an ask or deny rule for a durable guarantee. |

## Where the classifier reads configuration

The classifier reads the same [CLAUDE.md](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory.md) content Claude itself loads, so an instruction like "never force push" in your project's CLAUDE.md steers both Claude and the classifier at the same time. Start there for project conventions and behavioral rules.

For rules that apply across projects, such as trusted infrastructure or organization-wide deny rules, use the `autoMode` settings block. The classifier reads `autoMode` from the following scopes:

| Scope | File | Use for |
| :- | :- | :- |
| One developer | `~/.claude/settings.json` | Personal trusted infrastructure |
| Organization-wide | [Managed settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/server-managed-settings.md) | Trusted infrastructure distributed to all developers |
| `--settings` flag or Agent SDK | Inline JSON | Per-invocation overrides for automation |

The classifier doesn't read `autoMode` from project settings in `.claude/settings.json` or `.claude/settings.local.json`. Both files live in the repo directory, so a checked-in repo or a build step could otherwise inject its own allow rules. Move any `autoMode` block in `.claude/settings.local.json` to `~/.claude/settings.json`.

Entries from each scope are combined. A developer can extend `environment`, `allow`, `soft_deny`, and `hard_deny` with personal entries but can't remove entries that managed settings provide. Because allow rules act as exceptions to soft block rules inside the classifier, a developer-added `allow` entry can override an organization `soft_deny` entry: the combination is additive, not a hard policy boundary.

> [!NOTE]
>
> The classifier is a second gate that runs after the [permissions system](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions.md). For actions that must never run regardless of user intent or classifier configuration, use `permissions.deny` in managed settings, which blocks the action before the classifier is consulted and can't be overridden.

## Define trusted infrastructure

For most organizations, `autoMode.environment` is the only field you need to set. It tells the classifier which repos, buckets, and domains are trusted: the classifier uses it to decide what "external" means, so any destination not listed is a potential exfiltration target.

`claude auto-mode defaults` prints three kinds of environment entry.

* **Context slots**: describe your organization, stack, and security posture so the classifier reads the other rules in your context. Each defaults to `None configured` or to the conservative assumption named next to it:
  * **Organization**
  * **Primary use of Claude Code**: defaults to software development
  * **Cloud provider(s)**
  * **Repository visibility**: a repository is assumed private unless its remote host and name indicate otherwise, or the classifier reads a visibility check earlier in the conversation showing it is public.

    In the classifier requests sent by Claude Code itself, the classifier reads your messages and the commands Claude runs, not their output. The evidence has to be something the classifier can read, such as your own message naming the repository as public; the output of a `gh repo view` on its own doesn't reach it.
  * **Internal sharing / snippet hosting**: public paste and gist services are treated as outside the trust boundary until you name one
  * **Org-specific CLIs**
  * **Secrets management**
  * **CI/CD deploy targets**
  * **Network posture**
  * **Host containment**: defaults to an ordinary developer machine or CI runner with open internet. If Claude Code runs in a container, VM, or pod with an egress allow-list or neighbors it must not touch, name the allowed hosts, whether the cloud metadata endpoint should be reachable, and which cloud project, cluster, or registry the task uses and under what identity. Until this entry names that identity, the classifier [blocks](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md#what-the-classifier-blocks-by-default) requests for the host's own credentials. Requires Claude Code v2.1.257 or later
  * **Protected deployment namespaces / environments**: falls back to the Sensitive remote targets heuristic until you name them
  * **Data retention / declassification**
* **Trust slots**: name what the classifier treats as inside your boundary. The slots are Trusted repo, Source control, Trusted internal domains, Trusted cloud buckets, Key internal services, and Internal package registry. The repo and source-control entries default to the working repository and its configured remotes. Every other trust slot defaults to `None configured`, so nothing else is trusted until you add it. A repository's visibility scopes only confidential material: a private repository is an acceptable destination for confidential material, but making a repository private never clears secrets or personal or entrusted data into it, and the classifier treats content ported, repointed, or first read from outside the working repository as not that repository's own work.
* **Sensitivity slots**: name what the protective rules treat as high-risk. The slots are Sensitive data locations & audiences, Sensitive remote targets, and Protected IaC scopes. Each defaults to a broad heuristic, such as treating any host or namespace whose name carries `prod` or `production` as a sensitive remote target, so the protective rules are active before you configure anything. Naming concrete targets in a sensitivity slot makes those rules apply to the named targets instead of the heuristic.

To add your own entries alongside the defaults, include the literal string `"$defaults"` in the array. The default entries are spliced in at that position, so your custom entries can go before or after them.

The following example keeps the default entries and adds an organization's repos, buckets, domains, and services.

```json theme={null}
{
  "autoMode": {
    "environment": [
      "$defaults",
      "Source control: github.example.com/acme-corp and all repos under it",
      "Trusted cloud buckets: s3://acme-build-artifacts, gs://acme-ml-datasets",
      "Trusted internal domains: *.corp.example.com, api.internal.example.com",
      "Key internal services: Jenkins at ci.example.com, Artifactory at artifacts.example.com"
    ]
  }
}

After you save your settings, run claude auto-mode config to confirm the effective rules include your entries.

Entries are prose, not regex or tool patterns. The classifier reads them as natural-language rules. Write them the way you would describe your infrastructure to a new engineer. A thorough environment section covers:

  • Organization: your company name and what Claude Code is primarily used for, like software development, infrastructure automation, or data engineering
  • Source control: every GitHub, GitLab, or Bitbucket org your developers push to
  • Cloud providers and trusted buckets: bucket names or prefixes that Claude should be able to read from and write to
  • Trusted internal domains: hostnames for APIs, dashboards, and services inside your network, like *.internal.example.com
  • Key internal services: CI, artifact registries, internal package indexes, incident tooling
  • Internal package registry: the private npm, PyPI, or other registry that installs should route through, so installs that bypass it for a public registry get blocked
  • Sensitive data locations & audiences: the buckets, databases, or paths that hold personal data, confidential business data, credentials, regulated data, or similarly sensitive material, and the audiences that data in each location may be shared with, so the classifier protects those locations instead of guessing from content.
  • Sensitive remote targets: the namespaces, hosts, or containers that count as production, so remote shells and port-forwards into them need your explicit approval
  • Protected IaC scopes: the infrastructure resources whose apply or destroy should always require you to name the change
  • Additional context: regulated-industry constraints, multi-tenant infrastructure, or compliance requirements that affect what the classifier should treat as risky

A useful starting template: fill in the bracketed fields and remove any lines that don't apply.

```json theme={null} { "autoMode": { "environment": [ "$defaults", "Organization: {COMPANY_NAME}. Primary use: {PRIMARY_USE_CASE, e.g. software development, infrastructure automation}", "Source control: {SOURCE_CONTROL, e.g. GitHub org github.example.com/acme-corp}", "Cloud provider(s): {CLOUD_PROVIDERS, e.g. AWS, GCP, Azure}", "Trusted cloud buckets: {TRUSTED_BUCKETS, e.g. s3://acme-builds, gs://acme-datasets}", "Trusted internal domains: {TRUSTED_DOMAINS, e.g. *.internal.example.com, api.example.com}", "Key internal services: {SERVICES, e.g. Jenkins at ci.example.com, Artifactory at artifacts.example.com}", "Additional context: {EXTRA, e.g. regulated industry, multi-tenant infrastructure, compliance requirements}" ] } } 

You don't need to fill everything in at once. A reasonable rollout: start with the defaults and add your source control org and key internal services, which resolves the most common false positives like pushing to your own repos. Add trusted domains and cloud buckets next. Fill the rest as blocks come up.

## Generate environment entries with `/auto-mode-setup`

Run `/auto-mode-setup` to have Claude Code draft `autoMode.environment` entries, and sometimes [rule entries](#override-the-block-and-allow-rules) too, from your project and your recent sessions in it. If you accept the draft, Claude Code writes it to `~/.claude/settings.json`.

> [!NOTE]
>
> `/auto-mode-setup` is available on Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans and with a Claude Console API key. On a Pro, Max, or Team plan, you need v2.1.228 or later, or v2.1.233 or later on native Windows. On an Enterprise plan or with a Claude Console API key, you need v2.1.283 or later. If the command is missing from your session, see [`/auto-mode-setup` returns "Unknown command"](#auto-mode-setup-returns-unknown-command).

### What `/auto-mode-setup` reads

If `~/.claude/settings.json` already holds `autoMode` entries, Claude Code starts by asking whether to add to your environment list or replace it, and keeps the rules you wrote either way. Claude Code then asks how you use this project and offers two optional scans before it scans anything. In the scan, Claude Code always reads these sources:

* This project's `CLAUDE.md`, `README.md`, config files, and git remotes
* Your `autoMode` and `permissions.allow` settings
* The hosts, buckets, and command names from the commands Claude ran in your recent sessions in this project, never your messages

The two optional scans add one source each:

* The first word of each command in your shell history
* The remote hosts and names of the repositories under your home directory

### Review and save the draft

Claude Code scans in the background, then shows you the draft. You accept or discard it as a whole, so edit `~/.claude/settings.json` afterwards to adjust single entries. When you accept, Claude Code writes the draft and reconciles it with the settings you already have:

* Claude Code writes the `environment` list without `"$defaults"`, because the draft spells out the built-in entries it left unchanged
* Claude Code includes `"$defaults"` in each of the `allow`, `soft_deny`, and `hard_deny` lists the draft adds entries to, unless you already wrote an `allow` list without it, so the [built-in rules](#override-the-block-and-allow-rules) you haven't replaced stay in effect
* After saving, Claude Code offers to remove `permissions.allow` rules in `~/.claude/settings.json` that auto mode ignores, such as `Bash(*)`, or that auto-approve destructive commands

Then run `claude auto-mode config` to [see the effective result](#inspect-the-defaults-and-your-effective-config).

### Turn off `/auto-mode-setup`

Once auto mode has blocked several actions and you still have no `autoMode.environment` entries, Claude Code shows a dialog titled "Teach auto mode about your environment?" at the end of a turn and offers to run `/auto-mode-setup` for you. To stop the offer but keep the command, select **Don't show again** in that dialog.

To turn off both the command and the offer, add this [`skillOverrides`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills#override-skill-visibility-from-settings) entry to `~/.claude/settings.json`:

```json theme={null}
{
  "skillOverrides": {
    "auto-mode-setup": "off"
  }
}

/auto-mode-setup is a built-in command rather than a bundled skill, so this skillOverrides entry still applies to it, but disableBundledSkills doesn't turn it off.

docs.title: /auto-mode-setup returns "Unknown command"
docs.text:
If typing /auto-mode-setup at the Claude Code prompt prints Unknown command: /auto-mode-setup, check for these causes:

  • First session after an install or upgrade: start a new session. If the command is still missing there, see the setups where later sessions also start without it.
  • Outdated version: run claude --version in your shell. If the version is below the minimum for your plan, update Claude Code.
  • Telemetry off, third-party provider, or Claude apps gateway: before v2.1.304, the command isn't available in sessions where feature-flag fetching is off. If your session is one of them, update Claude Code to v2.1.304 or later.

In a cloud session, the command prints /auto-mode-setup isn't available in this environment. instead. Run it in an interactive session in your terminal.

docs.title: Override the block and allow rules
docs.text:
Three additional fields let you replace the classifier's built-in rule lists:

  • autoMode.hard_deny: unconditional security boundaries
  • autoMode.soft_deny: destructive actions that user intent can clear
  • autoMode.allow: exceptions to soft block rules

Each is an array of prose descriptions, read as natural-language rules. For tool-pattern-based hard blocks that run before the classifier, use permissions.deny.

Inside the classifier, precedence works in four tiers:

  • hard_deny rules block unconditionally. User intent and allow exceptions don't apply.
  • soft_deny rules block next. User intent and allow exceptions can override these.
  • allow rules then override matching soft_deny rules as exceptions.
  • Explicit user intent overrides the remaining soft blocks: if the user's message directly and specifically describes the exact action Claude is about to take, the classifier allows it even when a soft_deny rule matches.

General requests don't count as explicit intent. Asking Claude to "clean up the repo" doesn't authorize force-pushing, but asking Claude to "force-push this branch" does.

To loosen, add to allow when the classifier repeatedly flags a routine pattern the default exceptions don't cover. To tighten, add to soft_deny for destructive risks specific to your environment that the defaults miss, or to hard_deny for security boundaries that must never be crossed.

To keep the built-in rules while adding your own, include the literal string "$defaults" in the array. The default rules are spliced in at that position, so your custom rules can go before or after them, and you continue to inherit updates as the built-in list changes across releases.

The following example keeps the defaults in all four lists and adds organization-specific rules to each.

```json theme={null} { "autoMode": { "environment": [ "$defaults", "Source control: github.example.com/acme-corp and all repos under it" ], "allow": [ "$defaults", "Deploying to the staging namespace is allowed: staging is isolated from production and resets nightly", "Writing to s3://acme-scratch/ is allowed: ephemeral bucket with a 7-day lifecycle policy" ], "soft_deny": [ "$defaults", "Never run database migrations outside the migrations CLI, even against dev databases", "Never modify files under infra/terraform/prod/: production infrastructure changes go through the review workflow" ], "hard_deny": [ "$defaults", "Never send repository contents to third-party code-review APIs" ] } } 

> [!CAUTION]
>
> Setting any of `environment`, `allow`, `soft_deny`, or `hard_deny` without `"$defaults"` replaces the entire default list for that section. If you set an array without `"$defaults"`, you discard the built-in rules for that section:
>
> * `soft_deny`: every built-in soft block rule, including force push, `curl | bash`, production deploys, and auto-mode bypass
> * `hard_deny`: the built-in data exfiltration rule

Each section is evaluated independently, so setting `environment` alone leaves the default `allow`, `soft_deny`, and `hard_deny` lists intact.

Only omit `"$defaults"` when you intend to take full ownership of the list. To do that safely, run `claude auto-mode defaults` to print the built-in rules, copy them into your settings file, then review each rule against your own pipeline and risk tolerance.

## Edit rules from `/permissions`

To view and edit classifier rules and `environment` entries without opening a settings file, run [`/permissions`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions#manage-permissions) and select the **Auto mode** tab. The tab requires Claude Code v2.1.246 or later, and it appears only when [auto mode is available](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md#eliminate-prompts-with-auto-mode) to your session.

Claude Code shows entries from [managed settings](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/server-managed-settings.md) or the `--settings` flag as read-only, and saves every change you make on the tab to `~/.claude/settings.json`.

## Route all shell commands through the classifier

By default, narrow Bash and PowerShell allow rules such as `Bash(npm test)` stay in effect in auto mode. Claude Code resolves them before the classifier runs, unless the command carries [per-command allowed domains](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sandboxing.md#per-command-allowed-domains-in-auto-mode). Claude Code suspends only the broad rules that grant arbitrary code execution, such as `Bash(*)` or wildcarded interpreters, together with every rule that names [`Monitor`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference#monitor-tool), because Monitor commands run through the shell. This means a narrow rule can still let a destructive argument through without the classifier seeing it, for example a script path or flag the rule's prefix didn't anticipate.

Set `autoMode.classifyAllShell` to `true` to suspend every Bash and PowerShell allow rule while auto mode is active, so the classifier evaluates every shell command regardless of your allow list, except [critical-path removals](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md#critical-paths).

```json theme={null}
{
  "autoMode": {
    "classifyAllShell": true
  }
}

This trades latency for coverage: a command that an allow rule would have approved instantly now waits for a classifier decision, and each shell command counts as a classifier call.

The setting applies only while auto mode is active, and your allow rules behave normally in other permission modes.

docs.title: Inspect the defaults and your effective config
docs.text:
The claude auto-mode subcommands help you inspect, validate, and reset your configuration.

Print the built-in environment, allow, soft_deny, and hard_deny rules as JSON:

```bash theme={null} claude auto-mode defaults 

To read one rule's full wording without piping through `jq`, pass `--label` with the start of the rule's label, such as `claude auto-mode defaults --label 'Git Destructive'`. Matching is a case-insensitive prefix on each rule's label, and sections with no match print as empty lists.

Print what the classifier actually uses as JSON, with your settings applied where set and defaults otherwise:

```bash theme={null}
claude auto-mode config

Both defaults and config print the four rule lists as a single JSON object, with each rule as a prose string. This is a truncated example:

``json theme={null} { "allow": [ ... "Test Artifacts: Hardcoded test API keys, placeholder credentials in examples, or hardcoding test cases. Placeholder means authored as a placeholder — a file or value copied from a real secret or sensitive path is never a test artifact (see Sensitive-Source Provenance).", ... ], "soft_deny": [ "Git Destructive [named+specifics — **must name:** the destructive operation and its target]: Force pushing (git push --force), deleting remote branches, tags, or releases, or rewriting remote history. Alsogit commit --amendwhen the commit being rewritten is not the agent's own unpushed work: either no priorgit commitis visible (HEAD pre-dates the session), or agit pushof the current branch is visible after the most recent commit (it has been pushed). Clears when the user asked to amend/reword/fixup, or when it is a message-only reword (--amend -m …`, nothing newly staged) of a commit the agent visibly created this session.", ... ], "hard_deny": [...], "environment": [ ... "Trusted repo: The git repository the agent started in (its working directory) and its configured remote(s). When the repo's public/private visibility is given — by the Repository visibility entry or the user's own message — use it to scope what is OK to commit or push there: confidential material is fine in a private repo; in a public one, only that repo's own work is — and content ported, repointed, or first read from outside this session's repo is not its own work, whoever directed the port. Visibility scopes confidential material only: secrets and sensitive data (personal & entrusted) are never cleared into any repo by its visibility (see Definitions).", ... ] } 

Get AI feedback on your custom `allow`, `soft_deny`, `hard_deny`, and `environment` entries:

```bash theme={null}
claude auto-mode critique

If you've written custom rules, claude auto-mode critique reviews them and flags entries that are ambiguous, redundant, or likely to cause false positives.

To discard your customizations and return to the built-in defaults, run the reset subcommand, which removes the autoMode section from your user settings file:

bash theme={null} claude auto-mode reset

The command summarizes what it will remove and asks Reset auto mode configuration to defaults? before writing; pass --yes to skip the confirmation. Reset changes only ~/.claude/settings.json: autoMode rules from managed settings or the --settings flag still apply.

docs.title: Review denials
docs.text:
To review and retry actions the auto mode classifier denied, open /permissions and select the Recently denied tab, where Claude Code records each denial. Press r on a denied action to mark it for retry: when you exit the dialog, Claude Code sends a message telling the model it may retry that tool call and resumes the conversation.

When the classifier produces no verdict on the action, because a safety check separate from auto mode refused the classifier's own request or its response didn't parse, Claude Code denies the action without recording it under Recently denied. The linked error entry covers what Claude is told and how to run the action if you need it.

docs.title: Fix a denial with an allow rule, an environment entry, or a retry
docs.text:
To read the command or URL behind a notice such as bash denied by auto mode · [Data Exfiltration] · /permissions, use the Recently denied tab, a hook, or the conversation:

  • Recently denied tab: in the /permissions dialog, highlight a denied Bash or PowerShell action to read its command below the list. In screen reader mode, all the commands appear before the list instead.
  • Hook: to capture the exact input of denials programmatically, add a PermissionDenied hook, which receives it as tool_input.
  • Conversation: find the tool call. If the call appears shortened or folded into a summary line such as Ran 3 shell commands, press Ctrl+O to open the transcript viewer, which expands it.

The text beneath the call tells you whether there is anything to fix. A dim Not run · auto mode's check had no usable answer row, or text that reports a problem with the classifier itself, such as Auto mode could not evaluate this action, means Claude Code blocked the call without a verdict from the classifier. For a Not run row, press Ctrl+O to read the full message, then see Auto mode cannot determine the safety of an action or The server returned no safety verdict for what to do.

Otherwise, a line reading Denied by auto mode classifier with a reason such as [Production Deploy] or Blocked by classifier means the classifier judged the call unsafe, so pick the fix from what the call was trying to reach or do:

  • A destination Claude needs throughout the task, such as a package registry, an internal domain, or a repository host: add it to autoMode.environment.
  • A command you want to run without review from now on: add an allow rule.
  • A one-off action you did intend: state that intent in your next message and let Claude retry.

You can add the environment entry or allow rule from the /permissions dialog's Auto mode tab.

The text in square brackets, such as [Data Exfiltration], is the name of the rule the classifier matched. To read that rule's full wording, see Inspect the defaults and your effective config.

docs.title: Fix repeated denials
docs.text: Repeated denials for the same destination usually mean the classifier is missing context. Add that destination to autoMode.environment, or run /auto-mode-setup to have Claude Code draft the entries, then run claude auto-mode config to confirm the change took effect.

docs.title: Best practices for Claude Code
docs.text:
Get more out of Claude Code: tell Claude what it can't see, give it a check to run, and enforce the rules that can't have exceptions.

Claude Code is built in a way that, in most cases, your first plain prompt in a fresh session already does the right thing, without any setup on your part.

For example:

  • To let commands run safely without you approving each one, new terminal and VS Code sessions start in auto mode, where a classifier reviews anything risky before it runs.
  • To keep your main conversation focused while independent work happens in parallel, Claude delegates to subagents and checks in only when it has to.
  • To keep a long session going without you managing it, your conversation is compacted automatically before the context window fills.

This page covers what to do when the defaults aren't enough. That usually happens when your project has knowledge, rules, or constraints that Claude can't see from the code alone:

  • A deploy process that lives in someone's head
  • A file that must never be read
  • A check that has to pass before anything counts as done
  • A budget you need to stay under

No default can know those things about your project, so this is where a small amount of setup on your side pays off.

When a session doesn't go the way you expected, it's almost always one of these:

  • Claude built something different from what you had in mind, or it has to rediscover the same fact at the start of every session. It's missing information it can't get from reading the repo. See Tell Claude what it can't see.
  • Claude said it was done and it wasn't quite, usually because it had no way to check its own work. See Give Claude a check to run.
  • Claude did something that must never happen in this repo, or skipped a step that must always happen. A prompt alone can't guarantee either of those. See Enforce the rules that can't have exceptions.
  • Claude got it right, but it took more time, tokens, or permission prompts than the task was worth. See Change a default.

Let Claude run without you applies the same four points to unattended runs, and What you can stop doing lists the advice that current models have made unnecessary.

[!NOTE]

Setup for a whole team is on a separate page: Set up Claude Code for your organization.

docs.title: Deterministic and non-deterministic instructions
docs.text:
Every instruction you give Claude Code is one of these:

  1. Non-deterministic: you write the instruction, and Claude (the model) reads it. This can be your prompt, CLAUDE.md, or a skill. The model then decides what to do with this information. It usually follows your commands, and current models are good at understanding your intent without much context, but there's no guarantee that it'll follow your instructions. It can still decide not to do things, or do other things.
  2. Deterministic: you configure the instruction, and Claude Code (the harness) has to execute this. This can be a hook, a deny rule, or a managed setting. Claude Code applies this every time, no matter what the model decided to do.

Most things in Claude Code come in both forms:

Non-deterministic (Claude decides) Deterministic (Claude Code enforces) What to do Your prompt, CLAUDE.md, skills Claude picks up itself Hooks, and which skills only you can start What it can touch Auto mode's classifier Deny rules, the sandbox in strict mode, managed settings When it's done A request for evidence, /goal, /code-review Tests, typecheck, a Stop hook, CI How much it spends Effort level, Claude's own pace --max-turns or --max-budget-usd with -p, a spend limit you've set Who has the last word Claude's summary of what it did Branch protection, a person who approves the merge

Most of the time, you want Claude to decide. Almost every guideline has exceptions, and current models are good at reading the code in front of them and judging whether a guideline fits the situation. With the actual code in front of it, Claude is usually better placed to make that call than a rule you wrote in advance.

The deterministic kind is for when you want to make sure certain things always happen (or never happen), no matter what the model decides. This doesn't have to be anything dramatic. Auto mode already blocks the dramatic things, like a production deploy or a force push over someone's work. It's usually something specific to your project, and it can be as niche as you want it to be:

  • Never edit the generated client in src/gen/
  • Always run the license-header script after creating a file

You could've written either of these as a line in CLAUDE.md or in your prompt, and Claude would follow it nearly every time. But no matter how strongly you word it, whether Claude follows that line on a given turn is still Claude's call.

[!TIP]

If you keep adding emphasis to a CLAUDE.md line and Claude still misses it, that's a sign the line belongs in a hook. The reverse holds too: if you have hooks for things that are only preferences, delete them and let Claude decide.

docs.title: Tell Claude what it can't see
docs.text:
[!TIP]

Only write down what Claude can't find by reading the repo, or what it would otherwise spend time rediscovering every session.

Claude starts every task by reading your code, and current models are very good at this. They'll find your file layout, your conventions, your test framework, and how existing components are built, usually faster than you could explain them. That means Claude already knows most of what you might be tempted to write down for it.

What it can't find is the information that was never in the repo:

  • A decision your team made in a meeting
  • A deploy process that lives in one person's head
  • The environment variable your integration tests need

There's also information that is in the repo but takes a few minutes of digging to find, and Claude has to redo that digging at the start of every session.

A good test before you write anything down for Claude:

  1. Could it find this by reading the code?
  2. Would it actually go and look?

If both are yes, leave it out.

docs.title: Write a specific prompt
docs.text:
A specific prompt helps for the same reason, because it gives Claude information it doesn't already have. If you name the file, describe the symptom, and say what "fixed" looks like up front, you usually save yourself a round of corrections later.

The same goes for a preference between two reasonable approaches: Claude can't read that from the code, so if you care which one it picks, say so up front.

Instead of Try "fix the login bug" "users report login fails after the session times out. look at token refresh in src/auth/, write a failing test that reproduces it, then fix it" "add a calendar widget" "follow the pattern in HotDogWidget.php and build a calendar widget that lets you pick a month and page between years. no new libraries"

If you already have the thing Claude needs, hand it over instead of describing it:

  • A file: type @ and the path to include the file contents in your message.
  • An image: paste the screenshot of the design or the error into the prompt.
  • Command output: pipe it in from your shell with cat error.log | claude -p "what's going on here".

Phrases like think step by step or be thorough are ordinary prompt text rather than keywords. The main control for how hard Claude thinks is the effort level, which Change the model and effort covers. Wording like that can still nudge Claude within its effort setting, but it won't lift it past it.

One phrase that does still help is be ambitious. Claude tends to read a request conservatively and build the smallest thing that satisfies it, since it can't see how much you were hoping for. When you want the fuller version, with the edge cases handled and the natural follow-on included, say so:

```text theme={null} build the settings page from the mockup. be ambitious: empty and error states, the save flow wired up, keyboard navigation, not just the layout 

That's telling Claude about scope, which only you know, rather than how hard to think.

And when you're exploring rather than fixing something specific, a vague prompt like `what would you improve in this file?` is completely fine. You'll correct a bit more as you go, and that's the trade-off.

### Brainstorm with Claude first

When you don't know exactly what you want yet, you don't have to work it all out before you prompt. Ask Claude to interview you instead:

```text theme={null}
I want to add rate limiting to the public API but haven't thought it through yet. Interview me until you could write the spec, then write it to SPEC.md.

Claude comes back with multiple-choice questions about the parts you haven't pinned down: per-user versus per-key limits, what happens to requests over the limit, what's out of scope. It keeps asking until the answers add up to a spec.

Once SPEC.md exists, start a fresh session to build from it, so the build begins with a clean context and a written definition of done. It's also the file you'll point the reviewer at later, in Give Claude a check to run.

docs.title: Keep CLAUDE.md short
docs.text:
Claude Code loads CLAUDE.md into every session, which means every line in it takes a little of Claude's attention on every task, whether it's relevant or not. That's why the file works best when it only holds what Claude couldn't work out from the code itself:

  • How to confirm work in this repo: the exact test, typecheck, and lint commands, and how to run a single test file
  • Places where the code is misleading: an old pattern that's everywhere but that new code must not copy, or a directory that looks unused but isn't
  • Decisions that aren't in the repo: which error helper the team settled on, how deploys work, what needs a migration review
  • Anything you've had to correct twice already

A CLAUDE.md that passes that test stays short:

```markdown CLAUDE.md theme={null}

docs.title: Commands
docs.text:
• Install: pnpm install
  • Run one test file: pnpm vitest run path/to/file.test.ts
  • Typecheck: pnpm tsc --noEmit

docs.title: Conventions
docs.text:
• Use the error helpers in src/lib/errors.ts, never throw raw strings
  • src/legacy/ is still live but don't copy its patterns into new code

docs.title: Gotchas
docs.text:
• Integration tests need DATABASE_URL set, see .env.example 
    In a session, run `/context` to confirm that Claude loaded the file.

Notice that the typecheck line is only the command. Claude needs to know the command so it can check its own work as it goes. If you also want Claude Code to *enforce* a passing typecheck before Claude finishes, that's a job for a [`Stop` hook](#enforce-the-check-with-a-stop-hook). A line like `Always typecheck before you finish` in this file works most of the time, not every time.

You don't have to write the file from scratch:

* `/init` generates a starting version from your codebase. From there the work is mostly removing lines. The [memory guide](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory.md#write-effective-instructions) recommends staying under 200.
* `/doctor` suggests cuts for anything Claude can [already work out from the code](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory.md#my-claude-md-is-too-large).
* `/doctor prompt-audit` flags instructions that were written for older models, point at files that no longer exist, or [contradict each other](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory.md#audit-your-instruction-files).

Your personal preferences go in `CLAUDE.local.md` instead of `CLAUDE.md`, and you add that file to `.gitignore` so it stays out of the repo.

> [!NOTE]
>
> If Claude keeps ignoring a line that *is* in `CLAUDE.md`, adding IMPORTANT probably won't fix it. Either the file has grown long enough that the line gets lost, or the line is a rule that can't have exceptions, in which case it belongs in a [hook](#enforce-the-rules-that-cant-have-exceptions).

### Scope rules to one part of the codebase

If a rule only matters in one part of the codebase, put it in [`.claude/rules/`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory#path-specific-rules) with a `paths:` filter so it only loads when Claude is actually working there. For example, this `.claude/rules/api.md` loads for TypeScript files under `src/api/`:

```markdown .claude/rules/api.md theme={null}
---
paths:
  - "src/api/**/*.ts"
---
- Validate request bodies with the zod schemas in src/api/schemas/, don't hand-roll checks
- Every new endpoint needs an entry in openapi.yaml, CI fails without it

docs.title: Put team procedures in skills
docs.text:
A more capable model knows more about engineering, but not how your team does a release, what your incident runbook says, or how you want API docs written. That kind of knowledge goes in a skill: a procedure or a piece of team knowledge saved at .claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md.

Skills are also lighter on context than CLAUDE.md for this kind of thing. For a skill Claude can start on its own, it sees the name and description in every session, but only reads the full file when the task calls for it. A long release procedure sitting in a skill doesn't weigh on your unrelated bug fix the way it would in CLAUDE.md.

[!NOTE]

The CLAUDE.md rule applies to skills too: only write down what Claude can't find on its own.

For a workflow with side effects, like actually cutting that release, add disable-model-invocation: true. Claude then can't start the skill on its own, and it only runs when you type /release yourself. Saved as .claude/skills/release/SKILL.md, it could look like this:

docs.title: ```markdown .claude/skills/release/SKILL.md theme={null}
docs.text:
name: release description: Cut a new release. Bumps the version, writes the changelog entry, tags it and pushes the tag so CI can publish. disable-model-invocation: true

  1. Make sure you're on main with a clean tree. If not, stop and ask.
  2. Run pnpm changeset version and commit the result.
  3. Summarize the PRs merged since the last tag into CHANGELOG.md, one line each, user-facing changes only.
  4. Tag v<new version> and push the tag. CI publishes from there, never publish from your machine. 
    ### Connect the tools Claude needs

Some of what Claude can't see lives in another system entirely, like your issue tracker or your error dashboard. If that system has a CLI, that's usually the easiest way in. With `gh` installed and signed in, for example, Claude will open pull requests and read review comments without any explanation from you. For a CLI it hasn't seen before, pointing it at `--help` is enough.

For systems without a CLI, there's [MCP](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/mcp.md). You add a server from your shell:

```bash theme={null}
claude mcp add --transport http notion https://mcp.notion.com/mcp

The server then shows up under /mcp inside a session. Connected servers add their tool names and instructions to the context even when you're not using them, so it's worth turning off the ones you don't need there.

And if you work in a typed language, a code intelligence plugin lets Claude jump straight to a definition instead of reading through many files to find it.

docs.title: Give Claude a check to run
docs.text:
Claude stops when the work looks done. If it has nothing to run that tells it whether the work actually is done, "looks done" is all it has to go on. In practice that makes you the test suite, and every mistake sits there until you happen to notice it.

If you give it something that comes back pass or fail, Claude can close that loop itself. It makes the change, runs the check, and if something broke it reads the output and fixes it before running the check again.

[!TIP]

Give Claude something it can run that comes back pass or fail. Once it has that, it can keep going on its own and you don't have to watch.

The check can be almost anything, as long as Claude can read the result:

  • A test file
  • A build's exit code
  • A linter
  • A script that diffs output against a fixture
  • A browser screenshot next to the mockup

If your repo already has one of these, the single most useful line in your CLAUDE.md is the command that runs it.

How strict you make the check is up to you. The options go from Claude deciding for itself all the way to Claude Code enforcing it:

  • In the prompt: run the auth tests after, and keep going until they pass. Claude decides for itself when it's satisfied. This works for any task, today, with no setup.
  • As a goal: /goal all tests in tests/auth pass and lint is clean sets a condition that a separate model checks against the conversation after every turn, and Claude keeps going until it's met. You rarely need this in the session yourself. It matters for long background runs, where Claude sometimes ends a turn with a progress summary while items are still open, and the goal sends it back.
  • As a Stop hook: a Stop hook runs your script whenever Claude tries to end its turn, and sends Claude back to work if the script exits with code 2. This one is enforced by Claude Code (the harness), so the turn doesn't end until the typecheck passes or the block limit is reached. There's an example further down.
  • By someone who didn't write the code: in the terminal, /code-review reviews the diff in a fresh subagent that never saw your conversation. It isn't swayed by the reasoning that produced the code.

Whichever option you use, ask Claude for evidence: the command it ran and its output, or the screenshot. "All tests pass" on its own tells you very little, and reading the output is faster than rerunning the check yourself. For a session you weren't watching, it's also the only evidence you have.

[!TIP]

Once Claude says it's done, you can also run /verify in the session, which has Claude build and run the app and look at the result. That catches the kind of problem that tests and typechecks miss.

docs.title: Review against your spec
docs.text:
If you'd rather have the review check the work against your plan than hunt for bugs in general, write the review prompt yourself:

```text theme={null} use a subagent to review the rate limiter diff against SPEC.md, check every requirement is implemented and the listed edge cases have tests, report gaps that affect correctness and skip style 

> [!NOTE]
>
> Don't drop the `skip style` part of that prompt. A reviewer that's asked to find problems will always find *something*. If you fix every finding, you end up with extra abstraction layers and tests for cases that can't happen.

### Enforce the check with a Stop hook

The `Stop` hook version of the typecheck rule is a few lines in `.claude/settings.json`. Exit code 2 is what blocks the stop. Whatever the command prints to stderr goes back to Claude as the reason it can't finish yet, which is why the compiler output is redirected there:

```json .claude/settings.json theme={null}
{
  "hooks": {
    "Stop": [
      {
        "hooks": [
          { "type": "command", "command": "pnpm tsc --noEmit 1>&2 || exit 2" }
        ]
      }
    ]
  }
}

To see it work, ask Claude for a change that breaks a type: instead of finishing, it gets the compiler errors back and keeps going until tsc passes. If the hook blocks eight stops in a row with no tool call between them, Claude Code overrides the next block and ends the turn. To raise the cap, set CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP.

docs.title: Enforce the rules that can't have exceptions
docs.text:
[!TIP]

If something has to happen every time, make it a hook, a deny rule, or a managed setting. CLAUDE.md is for guidelines, and Claude is allowed to decide a guideline doesn't apply.

Take three rules you might have in CLAUDE.md today: Never read .env, Always run the formatter after editing, Don't touch the migrations folder. Claude will follow these almost every time. For the few where "almost" isn't good enough, move them out of CLAUDE.md and into configuration that Claude Code (the harness) applies itself. From then on, the outcome doesn't depend on what the model remembers or decides.

docs.title: Enforce steps with hooks
docs.text:
Hooks run something of yours at fixed points in Claude's loop: before or after a tool call, when Claude tries to stop, when a session starts, and so on. That something can be:

  • A shell command (the usual case)
  • A POST to an HTTP endpoint
  • A tool call on one of your MCP servers
  • A prompt or agent hook, which lets a model decide

A prompt or agent hook asks another model to decide, so it isn't deterministic either. For real enforcement, use a command or http hook, and add onFailure: "block" if the action should also be stopped when the hook itself crashes or times out. For a hook that scans commits for secrets, say, you'd rather block the commit than let it through unscanned while the scanner is down.

Here's the formatter rule as a PostToolUse hook. It runs after every Edit or Write, and whether Claude remembers the rule no longer matters, because Claude isn't the one running it:

```json .claude/settings.json theme={null} { "hooks": { "PostToolUse": [ { "matcher": "Edit|Write", "hooks": [ { "type": "command", "command": "npx prettier --write --ignore-unknown \"$(jq -r '.tool_input.file_path')\"" } ] } ] } } 

To check the hook, ask Claude to add a badly indented line to a file Prettier formats. The saved file comes back with the indentation fixed.

The migrations rule becomes a [`PreToolUse` hook](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks-guide#block-edits-to-protected-files) that exits with code 2 for any path under `migrations/`. You don't have to write it yourself: `write a hook that blocks edits to the migrations folder` works as a prompt, and `/hooks` shows the result. Don't overdo it, though: a hook is for a rule with *zero* exceptions, and `Prefer named exports` has plenty, so that one stays in `CLAUDE.md`.

### Limit access with permission rules and the sandbox

[Permission rules](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permissions.md) decide what Claude is allowed to run, read, and fetch. `deny` rules hold in every permission mode, including auto and `bypassPermissions`, which is exactly why the `.env` rule belongs there:

```json .claude/settings.json theme={null}
{
  "permissions": {
    "allow": ["Bash(pnpm tsc --noEmit)"],
    "ask": ["Bash(git push *)"],
    "deny": ["Read(./.env)", "Read(./.env.local)", "Read(./secrets/**)"]
  }
}

With this saved, asking Claude what's in .env fails, through the Read tool and through cat .env alike.

Rules match tool calls, not intent, so it's worth knowing where the edges are:

  • The Read rule does catch cat .env, because Claude Code recognizes the common file-reading commands.
  • It won't catch a script that opens the file.
  • A WebFetch deny rule for a domain does nothing about curl to that same domain, unless the sandbox is on.

For an OS-level limit on filesystem or network access, turn on the sandbox with /sandbox in a session. It confines Claude's shell commands on macOS, Linux, and WSL2 and picks up your Read deny rules and WebFetch(domain:...) rules too, so for anything security-related you want both.

By default Claude can still ask to retry a blocked command outside the sandbox, and that request goes through the normal permission flow. Strict sandbox mode, in the /sandbox Overrides tab, turns that retry off.

[!WARNING]

Auto mode is a classifier model judging each action rather than a hard rule. It's good at that, but like any judgment call it can be wrong. You can also tune what it treats as risky, and your org can turn it off entirely, so your "never" rules belong in deny rules or hooks.

docs.title: Choose who a rule applies to
docs.text:
Where a rule lives decides who it applies to:

  • .claude/settings.local.json and ~/.claude/settings.json are yours alone. When you select Yes, and don't ask again for a command, Claude Code saves that rule to the local file.
  • .claude/settings.json and the hooks in it belong to the repo. Once you commit them, they apply to everyone who works in the repo. Its deny rules apply right away. Its allow rules wait until each person accepts the trust dialog for that folder, and workspace trust also decides when its hooks start running on their machine.
  • Managed settings belong to the organization. They come from the admin console, MDM, or a managed-settings.json file, and no personal settings file can override them, which makes them the only place for a security team's policy. If you are the person who sets them, see Set up Claude Code for your organization.

Whatever the scope, keep the enforced set small. Every hook and deny rule will occasionally fire when it shouldn't, and someone has to maintain each one. If you ever find yourself at forty of them, most are probably preferences that Claude could have weighed on its own.

docs.title: Change a default
docs.text:
[!TIP]

The defaults are good enough to leave alone until a task costs more time, tokens, or interruptions than it should. When that happens, run /usage in the session to see where it went.

A new session already makes a handful of decisions for you:

  • Interactive terminal and VS Code sessions start in auto mode.
  • It runs Claude Opus 5.5 at medium effort on most plans and providers.
  • It delegates work to subagents when it sees a reason to.
  • It compacts the conversation as it grows.

Most of the time you never think about these. When a task does cost more than it should, one of these four is usually why.

docs.title: Change the permission mode
docs.text:
Both ends of the permission range have a cost:

  • Manual mode: you approve every edit and every command that isn't read-only yourself. Safe, but after the tenth prompt you start approving without reading, and nothing moves while you're away from the keyboard.
  • bypassPermissions: approves everything your deny and ask rules don't cover, which only makes sense in a disposable container.

Auto mode sits between the two, and it's what interactive terminal and VS Code sessions start in. Claude works without stopping for routine approvals, and a separate classifier model checks actions in a fixed order before they run. It concentrates on the things you'd want a person to stop:

  • curl | bash
  • Production deploys and migrations
  • Force pushes over other people's work
  • Sensitive data sent to external endpoints
  • Actions that look driven by content Claude read rather than by you

When it does block something, you get a notification and the action shows up under Recently denied in /permissions, where you can retry it with a manual approval. After three blocks in a row (or twenty in total), auto mode pauses and goes back to asking you.

None of this replaces your deterministic controls, because it runs after them. Deny and ask rules and PreToolUse hooks apply before the classifier sees anything, so a deny rule blocks in auto mode exactly like it does everywhere else. The sandbox still confines the shell commands it wraps.

[!NOTE]

You can also say don't push until I've reviewed in the conversation, and the classifier treats that as a block signal. It's still a model reading the transcript, and the sentence can get lost when the conversation compacts, so anything that matters belongs in a deny rule.

The opposite problem is the classifier repeatedly stopping something that's routine in your setup. Rather than approving it manually every time, add it to autoMode.allow or describe your trusted infrastructure in the auto mode configuration. It's plain English rather than patterns, and /auto-mode-setup can draft the environment part for you from your project and recent sessions:

```json ~/.claude/settings.json theme={null} { "autoMode": { "environment": [ "$defaults", "Source control: github.com/example-org and every repo under it", "Trusted internal domains: *.internal.example.com" ], "allow": [ "$defaults", "Deploying to the staging namespace is fine, it's isolated from production and resets nightly" ] } } 

> [!WARNING]
>
> Keep `"$defaults"` in every list you set, because without it your entries *replace* that list's built-in rules instead of adding to them. For `environment` and `allow` you'd lose the built-in context and exceptions, and a `soft_deny` list without it drops the built-in blocks on force pushes and production deploys.
>
> The `autoMode` block also has to live in `~/.claude/settings.json` rather than the project, because the classifier ignores `autoMode` in project settings.

If you'd rather see every edit and command before it happens, `Shift+Tab` in the session cycles through the permission modes, Manual included, or start with `claude --permission-mode manual` from your shell. And if Manual then asks too often, `/fewer-permission-prompts` scans your recent transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP calls and adds them to an allowlist in `.claude/settings.json`.

### Change the model and effort

[Effort](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#adjust-effort-level) is the main control for how long Claude thinks, and it replaces most of what people used to do with prompt wording. Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 default to `medium`, which is plenty for everyday feature work with a clear scope. The times you'd move it, with `/effort` in the session:

* Raise it with `/effort high` or `/effort xhigh` when getting it right depends on cases that are quick to overlook. Think of a bug in code you didn't write, a flaky test, or a schema change where Claude has to find every reader of the old shape. Claude then checks more edge cases and verifies more of its work before answering, which is where the extra time and tokens go.
* Lower it with `/effort low` when you're going back and forth quickly and reviewing each result anyway: brainstorming, a first sketch, a rename across a few files. Claude gets you a starting point sooner, and since you're steering every step, the extra deliberation wouldn't have changed much besides the wait.
* Save `max` for a hard problem you want Claude to work through without you, like hunting for a security vulnerability. On ordinary tasks it tends to overthink, so you pay more for an answer that may be no better than `high` would have given you.
* When only the next message needs it, like one tricky question in the middle of otherwise routine work, put [`ultrathink`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config#use-ultrathink-for-one-off-deep-reasoning) in that prompt instead of changing the setting.

For the model itself, the default Opus 5.5 handles most coding well and Sonnet costs less on routine work. [Claude Fable 5.1](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#work-with-fable) is there when you select it explicitly with `/model fable`, and Haiku is a good fit for subagents doing simple jobs. [Model configuration](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md) has the full list per plan and provider.

### Know what subagents cost

Claude delegates to [subagents](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md) on its own:

* Broad codebase searches go to the built-in Explore agent.
* Side tasks get [forked](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md#fork-the-current-conversation) while fork mode is on (the default).
* The subagents it starts run in the background by default, so your main conversation keeps moving.

You rarely need to ask for any of this, but it helps to know what you're getting and what it costs.

Subagents pay off in these situations:

* Running independent pieces of work at the same time, so the whole task finishes sooner
* Keeping long output, like a full test run or a wide search, out of your main conversation, where it would otherwise ride along for the rest of the session
* Getting a reviewer that hasn't seen how the code was written
* Giving a task fewer tools than the main session has, like a reviewer that can read but not edit

What they cost you is mostly tokens, since every subagent sends its own requests and they count against the same usage as your main conversation. Sometimes it's time as well: a fresh subagent first has to gather context your conversation already had, so it can end up *slower* than doing the task where you are.

And by default it's the same model (or a smaller one) on the same task. You get parallelism or a fresh pair of eyes out of it, but not a smarter answer.

To spend less on them:

* Set [`model: haiku`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents#choose-a-model) in a subagent's definition if its work is simple, like collecting the files that import a module or checking links in the docs. That kind of job doesn't need the bigger model, and Haiku costs a lot less per request.
* Ask for short summaries back, so twenty results don't fill your context anyway.
* Check `/usage` to see what share of your usage each subagent type takes, so you can tell which ones are earning their cost.
* Give a custom subagent in `.claude/agents/` only `tools: Read, Grep, Glob`. Now it's a reviewer that can't edit anything, and that limit is enforced by Claude Code rather than requested in a prompt.

That reviewer is one short file, `.claude/agents/reviewer.md`:

```markdown .claude/agents/reviewer.md theme={null}
---
name: reviewer
description: Reviews changed files against the spec they were built from. Use after implementing a feature, before opening the PR.
tools: Read, Grep, Glob
---
You're reviewing code you didn't write. Compare the changed files against the spec you're given,
check that every requirement is implemented and the listed edge cases have tests,
and report only the gaps that affect correctness. Skip style.

Ask Claude to have the reviewer compare the rate limiter against SPEC.md and the gaps come back into your session, where Claude can fix them.

docs.title: Keep cost and context down
docs.text:
With a 1M-token window on most current models and compaction near the top of it, you'll rarely run out of context. You can still pay for context you don't need, though. Every request sends the whole conversation, so a session that's collected three unrelated tasks re-reads all three on every turn of the fourth. That's discounted while the cache is warm and full price once it expires.

/usage is the first place to look. On Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise it breaks your usage down by skill, subagent, plugin, and MCP server. It also flags patterns like long context or frequent cache misses once one of them passes 10% of your usage. From there, the usual fixes:

  • /clear between unrelated tasks. It costs nothing, and it means the next task doesn't keep paying for the previous one's history. /clear oauth-migration names the session you're leaving, so you can come back to it later.
  • /compact with a focus, like /compact keep the API changes and the test commands. On a long session /compact is itself a big request, since it reads the whole conversation to summarize it, and even more so once the cache has expired.
  • Keep an eye on background work: a /loop, a goal's check after every turn, and Claude's own subagents all keep sending requests while you aren't typing.

[!NOTE]

The prompt cache lasts about an hour on a subscription and five minutes on an API key, cloud provider, or usage credits. Subagents get five minutes unless you change it.

On the one-hour cache, a session past about 200K tokens that sits idle is compacted shortly before the cache expires, so after lunch you continue from a summary. If you don't need the history at all, a fresh session still costs less.

docs.title: Steer the session
docs.text:
[!TIP]

Watch the first minute, press Esc the moment Claude drifts, and after two failed corrections run /clear and write a better prompt instead of a third.

No amount of configuration replaces watching the first minute and stepping in when Claude heads somewhere you didn't intend. There are only a few controls for that, and they're worth knowing by heart:

  • Esc stops Claude mid-action and keeps everything up to that point, so you can redirect without losing work.
  • /rewind, or Esc twice on an empty prompt, opens the rewind menu, where you roll the code, the conversation, or both back to an earlier prompt. That makes it low-risk to try the bolder approach first and rewind if it doesn't work out. The same menu can also summarize part of the conversation when it has gone stale.
  • /clear starts over. If you've corrected the same thing twice and it's still wrong, a third correction mostly adds to a conversation that already contains two failed attempts for Claude to keep re-reading. /clear plus one new prompt that folds in what you learned works better almost every time.

[!WARNING]

Checkpoints cover the files Claude edited with its own file tools in your main conversation, so a file that only a Bash command touched isn't restored. They work alongside git rather than replacing it.

Two smaller ones: /btw answers a quick question without adding anything to the history. And for work that spans several days, /rename oauth-migration in the session names it, so that claude --resume oauth-migration from your shell picks it back up later, checkpoints included. claude --continue resumes the most recent one.

docs.title: Let Claude run without you
docs.text:
[!TIP]

Before a run goes unattended, make sure it knows what done looks like, can check its own work, and can only touch what it should. Give it a cap on turns or spend, and have a person approve the result at the end.

Everything on this page matters a little more once you're not around to catch mistakes. While you're watching, Claude missing some piece of context isn't a big deal: you notice within a message or two and tell it. In a run you started before going to bed, nobody tells it, and you find out the next morning that it spent the whole night building on the wrong assumption.

Before you leave a task running on its own, it's worth going through these five questions with that specific task in mind:

  1. Does it know what done looks like? A goal condition, a spec file, or a failing test it has to turn green.
  2. Can it check its own work? The test suite, a Stop hook, some kind of review step.
  3. What's it allowed to touch? Permission rules, dontAsk, the sandbox, a worktree, the one branch it may push to.
  4. What stops it? --max-turns, --max-budget-usd, a spend limit.
  5. Where does the result go, and who signs off? A PR, a comment, or a summary, and then a person approving the merge, the deploy, or anything else you can't take back.

Once it's going, Claude will carry a long task through on its own. The parts that stay with you are starting it, deciding what "done" means this time, and approving the merge at the end.

docs.title: Run Claude from a script
docs.text:
claude -p "prompt" runs once and exits, which is how Claude Code ends up in CI jobs, git hooks, and shell loops.

In a script you'll almost always want a few more flags:

  • --bare skips hooks, skills, plugins, MCP servers, and CLAUDE.md files, the repo's as well as the machine's, so the run does the same thing wherever it runs. It also never touches your claude.ai login: auth comes from ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, an apiKeyHelper in the file you pass with --settings, or your cloud provider's credentials.
  • --append-system-prompt, --mcp-config, and --settings pass in whatever the run does need, explicitly.
  • --allowedTools pre-approves its tools, and --permission-mode dontAsk refuses anything else that would have prompted.
  • --output-format json gives you a single result object to parse, and stream-json with --verbose streams events as they happen.

Put together, that looks like this:

```bash theme={null} for file in $(cat files.txt); do claude --bare -p "Migrate $file to the new logger API and commit. Reply OK or FAIL." \ --allowedTools "Read,Edit,Bash(git add *),Bash(git commit *)" \ --permission-mode dontAsk \ --max-turns 20 done 

When a run finishes, Claude replies `OK` or `FAIL`, and a run that hits the turn limit exits with an error instead. Try it on three files first, see what goes wrong, fix the prompt, then run the rest.

Auto mode works with `-p` too if you pass `--permission-mode auto`. In a non-interactive run, a classifier block denies that one action and Claude carries on, and repeated blocks don't pause the run the way they do in a terminal. Read [how the thresholds apply there](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md#repeated-block-thresholds) before you rely on it.

### Start runs on a schedule or an event

Once a run is going, Claude can handle the rest by itself. The one thing it can't do is decide to *start*, so something has to: you, a timer, or an event like a failed CI check or a new PR.

Inside an open session that's [`/loop`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/scheduled-tasks#run-a-prompt-repeatedly-with-%2Floop), which repeats a prompt on an interval:

```text theme={null}
/loop 15m check CI on this branch, and if it's red pull the failing job's log, fix it and push

Each run is another turn in the same session, so don't leave one going in a long conversation. For anything that should happen while your laptop is closed, /schedule sets up a cloud scheduled task that runs on a timer. It needs a claude.ai login rather than an API key. You can add a GitHub-event trigger by asking Claude, or an API trigger at claude.ai/code/routines.

[!WARNING]

Before you leave a cloud scheduled task running, protect main with a GitHub branch rule the task can't bypass. And watch the first few runs of anything new before trusting it unattended.

docs.title: Run sessions in parallel
docs.text:
When you have separate pieces of work going at once, give each its own checkout so the edits can't collide. claude -w feature-auth starts a session in a new worktree, the desktop app runs several of these side by side, and cloud sessions run them in the cloud instead of on your machine.

A worktree is a fresh checkout, which means gitignored files like .env aren't there and dependencies aren't installed. For the first, list the gitignored files you need in a .worktreeinclude at the repo root (same syntax as .gitignore) and Claude Code copies them into every worktree it creates:

text .worktreeinclude theme={null} .env .env.local config/dev-credentials.json

Keep it to small files: it copies rather than links, so node_modules in there would mean a full copy per worktree. For large directories there's the worktree.symlinkDirectories setting, or keep the install command in CLAUDE.md so Claude runs it whenever it starts in a new checkout.

You rarely have to clean any of this up yourself:

  • When you exit an unnamed worktree session, Claude Code removes the worktree if there's nothing in it. For a named session, or one with changes, it asks what to do.
  • Subagent worktrees disappear when the subagent finishes without changes.
  • Subagent and background-session worktrees that do get left behind are swept once they're older than cleanupPeriodDays and hold no work.

[!NOTE]

A claude -p --worktree run is one you clean up yourself, since it exits without asking. Remove those with git worktree remove <path>, and if git refuses because the worktree is locked, git worktree unlock <path> first.

For one big mechanical change across many files, /batch migrate every handler to the v2 response helpers splits the work into 5 to 30 units and shows you the plan. Then it runs each unit in its own worktree and opens a PR for it. From your shell, claude agents (still a research preview) gives you one screen for everything running in the background on your machine.

A second session is also the easiest independent reviewer you can get. One session writes the rate limiter, another reviews @src/middleware/rateLimiter.ts without having watched it being written, and you paste the findings back into the first. Same idea as /code-review, with you carrying the messages.

docs.title: What you can stop doing
docs.text:
Every one of these was good advice when it was written. Most were workarounds for something the model couldn't reliably do yet, and the models have since caught up. If a few are still habits, here's why it's safe to drop them.

The old advice Why it's gone The context window is your main constraint, manage it aggressively Most current models have a 1M-token window and compaction happens on its own, so running out is rare. /clear between tasks is still worth doing, because a focused context gets you better answers and costs less. Add IMPORTANT or ALL CAPS to instructions Claude keeps missing Older models sometimes needed the emphasis. Current ones follow a plainly worded line, and piling on emphasis mostly makes Claude over-apply the rule. If it's a rule that can't bend, turn it into a hook or a deny rule. If the line is getting lost in a long file, the file needs to be shorter. Use subagents to protect your context window Running out of context is rarely the problem anymore. Subagents are still great for parallel work, keeping noisy output out of your way, and independent review, but each of those costs extra tokens. Delegate to a subagent for a better answer Handing the same task to a subagent doesn't make the answer any better. A fresh reviewer does help, because it hasn't seen your reasoning, which is a different thing from delegating. think hard, think harder, be thorough in the prompt Effort is the control for that. Those phrases are ordinary prompt text that nudges Claude within its effort setting rather than keywords that raise it. ultrathink still works: it asks for deeper reasoning on that single turn without touching your effort setting. Tell Claude to keep going, loop until done, don't be lazy Current models usually carry on through an agreed task without being told, and lines like that are more likely to cause over-work than fix a stall. Giving Claude a check to pass is different, and still worth doing. If a run does stop short, say continue, and for runs nobody's watching, /goal or a Stop hook enforces it. Describe your architecture and file layout in CLAUDE.md Claude reads the repo itself. Only write down what isn't in there.

If any other advice on this page ever starts to feel like busywork, that's probably a sign it belongs in this table too.
