docs.title: Review locally with /code-review
docs.text:
Run /code-review in a Claude Code session to find bugs in your branch's changes, point the review at a pull request or path, and have Claude apply the fixes.

/code-review is a command you type at the Claude Code prompt, in the session where you're working. Claude reviews the changes on your branch, looks for correctness bugs, and reports what it found in your conversation. Depending on your model and effort level, the review also covers reuse, simplification, and efficiency cleanups.

The command works on any plan. The review runs in your own session, so it counts toward your plan's usage or API billing the same way the rest of the session does.

[!NOTE]

To have every pull request in a repository reviewed automatically on GitHub, see Code Review, a managed service that an Owner turns on for your organization.

/review is an alias of /code-review. Before v2.1.223, /review was a separate command that ran a single-pass, read-only review of a GitHub pull request.

1. Run /code-review

Run the command:

```text theme={null} /code-review 

With no target, the review covers the changes on your current branch. To point the review at a pull request, another branch, a path, or a range of commits instead, see [Choose what to review](#choose-what-to-review).

You can also add flags:

* `--fix`: also asks Claude to apply the findings to your working tree after the review. Its edits go through your [permission mode](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/permission-modes.md).
* `--comment`: posts the findings on a GitHub pull request as inline comments, or on a [GitLab merge request](#post-findings-to-a-gitlab-merge-request) as a single note

**2. Keep working**

The review runs as a background [subagent](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/sub-agents.md) with its own context window, so it doesn't fill your conversation. The findings arrive in your conversation when the review completes.

**3. Act on the findings**

Ask Claude to fix what the review found. With `--fix` or `--comment`, Claude applies or posts the findings as part of the review, and you may be asked to approve its edits.

## Choose what to review

To review something other than your current branch, type a target after the effort level and any flags. Claude receives that text as the review target. A target can be a pull request number, a branch name, a file path, or a Git revision range. Find what you want reviewed in the first column and type what the second column shows:

| To point the review at | Type |
| :- | :- |
| Your current branch and uncommitted changes | `/code-review` |
| Your last 15 commits | `/code-review HEAD~15..HEAD` |
| One branch against another | `/code-review main...my-feature` |
| A single commit, where `abc1234` is the commit's hash | `/code-review abc1234^..abc1234` |
| A pull request by number | `/code-review 1234` |
| A file or directory path | `/code-review src/auth` |

With no target, `/code-review` reviews your branch's commits ahead of its upstream branch plus your uncommitted changes. If the branch has no upstream, Claude compares against `main`, or against the previous commit.

With `ultra`, Claude Code reads the target differently, as [Text after the effort level and flags](#text-after-the-effort-level-and-flags) describes.

## What the review reads and edits

Check these before you run a review, especially with `--fix`:

* **Edits**: without `--fix`, the review's instructions ask Claude for a report only. With `--fix`, they also ask it to apply the findings to your working tree. Either way, any edit goes through your permission mode.
* **Rewinding**: a background review applies its `--fix` edits outside your session's [checkpoints](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/checkpointing.md#subagent-edits-not-restored). After one, `/rewind` restores only the files Claude had already edited in your conversation. The review's edits to other files stay, so use git to revert them. When the review [runs in the foreground](#run-in-the-foreground), it edits your working tree during your own turn, so `/rewind` restores its edits as usual.
* **Instructions**: the review follows your `CLAUDE.md`, including in a non-interactive `-p` run. It doesn't read `REVIEW.md`. That file configures the managed [Code Review service](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review-customize.md#use-review-md-for-review-only-rules) on GitHub pull requests.

## How findings are reported

Claude reports the findings as text in the reply in both of these runs:

* In a terminal session, where `/code-review` runs the review as a [forked subagent](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills.md#run-skills-in-a-subagent)
* In a `-p` run with text or JSON output

In a host application that requests the findings list, such as the [desktop app](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop.md#review-your-code), Claude reports the review's findings through the [`ReportFindings` tool](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/tools-reference) instead. The report appears as a findings list, and each entry shows the file location, a one-sentence summary, and a category tag such as `correctness` when the finding carries one. A host request applies at every effort level and requires Claude Code v2.1.218 or later.

When Claude fixes reported findings later in the session, it reports them again. Claude Code then marks each finding in the updated findings list as fixed, skipped, or no change needed.

## Tune effort and arguments

Beyond `--fix` and `--comment`, the command takes these flags:

* `--post`: on an `ultra` cloud review of a `github.com` pull request, preselects posting the finished findings to the PR in the launch dialog. See [Post findings to the pull request](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/ultrareview.md#post-findings-to-the-pull-request). Requires Claude Code v2.1.227 or later.
* `--max-findings <n>`, `--max-findings all`, or `--max-findings default`: reports up to `n` findings, or every finding with `all`, in place of the review's usual limit. Where the review reports through the findings tool, the limit is 32. Later reviews reuse the value you typed until you pass `--max-findings default`, but a value passed in a non-interactive `-p` run isn't remembered. Requires Claude Code v2.1.288 or later.

Pass an [effort level](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config.md#adjust-effort-level) to trade coverage for confidence. At `low`, the review reports the findings it's most confident in, so you see fewer false positives. From `medium` through `max`, the review broadens coverage.

When you don't type a level, the review reuses the last level from `low` through `max` you typed, even in an earlier session. Claude Code shows a notice such as `Reusing high effort, the level you typed last time`. These rules decide which level a run uses:

* **Typing a level**: a level you type, like `/code-review high`, changes what later runs reuse
* **Non-interactive runs**: a level you pass in a non-interactive `-p` run doesn't update the remembered level
* **`ultra`**: the review neither uses nor updates the remembered level
* **No level ever typed**: the review uses the session's current effort

Before v2.1.223, a `/code-review` without a level always used the session's current effort.

### Post findings to a GitLab merge request

When you pass `--comment` for a GitLab merge request, Claude Code posts the findings through GitLab's `glab` CLI. Requires Claude Code v2.1.257 or later. When `glab` isn't installed, Claude prints the findings in the terminal instead.

Pass the merge request as its URL or a `!123` reference. Claude Code treats a bare number or branch name as a merge request only when the checkout's origin is on `gitlab.com`. On a self-managed GitLab instance, pass the URL or `!123` form.

### Text after the effort level and flags

After the effort level and flags, Claude Code reads the rest of the line as the review target. The `ultra` argument changes that reading:

* **With `ultra`**: Claude Code reads a single word as a base branch or PR number. Longer text that doesn't name a branch or PR becomes [a note attached to the review](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/ultrareview.md#pass-a-request-in-plain-words). `/code-review ultra check my auth changes` reviews your current branch, and Claude relates the findings to your note.
* **Without `ultra`**: everything left is the review target, even when it starts with another command name. `/code-review /fix-issue 123` reviews with `/fix-issue 123` as target text instead of loading `/fix-issue` as a second [stacked skill](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills.md#stack-several-skills-in-one-message). Before v2.1.218, a command stacked after `/code-review` expanded as its own skill.

## Run in the foreground

To make the review run in the foreground, do one of these:

* Run it in non-interactive mode, with the `-p` flag or the Agent SDK. Claude Code waits for the review and includes the findings in the response, except for `ultra`, which [doesn't wait for the cloud review](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/ultrareview.md#run-ultrareview-non-interactively).
* Set [`CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_BACKGROUND_TASKS`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars) to `1`, which also turns off other background task features
* Run `/code-review` again while an earlier review is still in progress

Before v2.1.218, the review ran inside your conversation.

## Let Claude start the review

Claude can start `/code-review` on its own, without you typing the command:

* **When you ask in plain language**: ask Claude to review your changes and it can run the skill
* **From a scheduled task**: a [session-scoped scheduled task](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/scheduled-tasks.md) with `/code-review` as its prompt runs the review

A session-scoped scheduled task never launches the [cloud review](#escalate-to-ultrareview), so schedule `/code-review` without the `ultra` argument.

To stop both Claude and scheduled tasks from starting the review while keeping `/code-review` available for you to type, add a [`skillOverrides`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills#override-skill-visibility-from-settings) entry to a [settings file](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings.md#where-settings-live) such as `~/.claude/settings.json`:

```json theme={null}
{
  "skillOverrides": {
    "code-review": "user-invocable-only"
  }
}

Before v2.1.246, Claude started /code-review on its own only where a feature flag fetched from Anthropic turned it on. In sessions that don't fetch feature flags, /code-review ran only when you typed it, and a scheduled /code-review reached Claude as plain text.

docs.title: Escalate to ultrareview
docs.text:
/code-review ultra --fix runs the deeper ultrareview in the cloud, then asks Claude to apply its findings to your working tree when they arrive back in your session.

Ultrareview uses its own scope:

  • What it compares: your current branch against the repository's default branch, plus uncommitted and staged changes in the working tree
  • Sensitive files: for uncommitted changes to files named like credentials or keys, such as .env and *.tfvars files, Claude Code follows the rules for uploading a local repository to a cloud session
  • A different base: pass a branch name, such as /code-review ultra develop, to compare against a different base

When the target is a github.com pull request, you can have Claude post the finished findings to the PR as a comment from your GitHub account. Requires Claude Code v2.1.227 or later.

[!NOTE]

Ultrareview requires authentication with a claude.ai account. It isn't available on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry, or to organizations with Zero Data Retention enabled or with the HIPAA configuration applied. In these cases, /code-review ultra runs a local review in your session instead. Organizations that use customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) can't run ultrareview. To review your changes locally, run /code-review.

To run a cloud review from a script or CI job, use the claude ultrareview subcommand, which waits for the findings and prints them to stdout.

docs.title: Change or build on the review
docs.text:
/code-review is a bundled skill: its instructions are built into Claude Code, so there is no SKILL.md file on disk to open or edit. To give every review project rules to follow, add them to your CLAUDE.md. To go further, start from one of these pages:

  • Replace the command: a project or personal skill named code-review runs in place of the bundled one, and the /review alias keeps running the bundled review. See Resolve skills that share a name.
  • Build your own reviewer: write a reviewer subagent or a review skill
  • Use a neighboring command: /simplify reviews for cleanup only and applies its fixes, and /verify runs your app to confirm a change works

The command was named /simplify before v2.1.147, when it applied fixes by default. If you scripted /simplify for bug-finding, switch to /code-review --fix.

docs.title: Read and request reviews on a pull request
docs.text:
Read Code Review findings on your GitHub pull request, respond to or dismiss them, and request a review with @claude review.

Code Review is a managed service that an Owner in your Claude organization turns on for a set of GitHub repositories. Once it's on, Claude reviews pull requests in those repositories and posts its findings as inline comments, a summary in the review body, and a check run named Claude Code Review. A review never approves or blocks your pull request, and the check run never concludes as a failure.

An Owner controls when reviews run and how thorough they are for each repository.

[!NOTE]

If your plan doesn't include Code Review, you can still have Claude review your branch from a Claude Code session: see Review locally with /code-review.

docs.title: Severity levels
docs.text:
Claude posts each finding as an inline comment on the lines concerned and marks it with one of three severity levels:

Marker Severity Meaning 🔴 Important A bug that should be fixed before merging 🟡 Nit A minor issue, worth fixing but not blocking 🟣 Pre-existing A bug that exists in the codebase but wasn't introduced by this PR

When the review recorded its reasoning, the finding has a collapsed Why this was flagged section. Expand it to read why Claude flagged the issue and how it verified the problem.

To change what Claude flags in your repository or how it ranks severity, see Customize Code Review.

docs.title: Respond to findings
docs.text:
You can merge without responding to a finding, unless your repository's own rules require it. If its branch protection requires conversation resolution, resolve each finding's thread before you merge.

To clear a finding, resolve its thread or push a fix.

  • Dismiss it without a code change: resolve the thread yourself on GitHub. Replying alone doesn't dismiss a finding.
  • Fix the issue: change the code and push. The next review of the pull request resolves its earlier thread when it judges the issue fixed, whether that review runs automatically on your push or you request it.
  • Explain or disagree: reply to the comment. Claude doesn't respond right away, and a reply doesn't start a review. The next review of the pull request reads the replies on its earlier findings, and can resolve the thread or post one follow-up reply. If the same kind of finding keeps coming back, ask a maintainer to add a rule to REVIEW.md.

To get that next review without pushing, comment @claude review as a top-level pull request comment.

docs.title: Check run output
docs.text:
The Details link on the Claude Code Review check run opens the findings in one table sorted by severity, including any finding whose inline comment GitHub didn't accept:

Severity File:Line Issue 🔴 Important src/auth/session.ts:142 Token refresh races with logout, leaving stale sessions active 🟡 Nit src/auth/session.ts:88 parseExpiry silently returns 0 on malformed input

A finding that has a line but wasn't posted as an inline comment appears as an annotation in the Files changed tab, on the lines concerned. Important findings show in red, nits in yellow, and pre-existing bugs in gray.

The check run concludes as neutral, or as skipped after some pushes that change no files and keep the earlier result. It never concludes as a failure, so a finished review doesn't fail a required check. If you don't see findings, or a review didn't run, see Troubleshoot Code Review.

docs.title: When a push keeps the earlier result
docs.text:
If the check run has one of these titles after you push, Code Review kept the result of an earlier review instead of starting a new one:

  • Code review skipped — no new changes: no Important finding from the earlier review is still open, so you don't need a new review
  • Code review not repeated — earlier findings still open: to start a new review, push a fix for an open Important finding, or resolve its thread and push again

On github.com, Code Review can keep a result when both of these hold:

  • The pull request still adds and removes the same lines, as after an empty commit, a clean merge of the base branch, or a clean rebase
  • Nobody has resolved an Important finding's thread since that review

To get a review without a code change, comment @claude review or click Re-run on the check run.

docs.title: Read the result from a script
docs.text:
To gate a merge or post a summary from your own CI, parse the last line of the Details text with gh and jq. That line is an HTML comment that holds the severity counts as JSON:

```text theme={null}

The lines above it can include file names from the pull request. If you parse the text your own way, take the counts from the last line only, as the command in these steps does.

**1. Find the check run ID**

From your shell, list the commit's check runs and take the `id` of the `Claude Code Review` run. Replace `OWNER` and `REPO` with your repository owner and name, and `<commit-sha>` with the pull request's head commit:

```bash theme={null}
gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/commits/<commit-sha>/check-runs --jq '.check_runs[] | {id, name}'

If the commit has had more than one Claude Code Review run, such as after a Re-run, GitHub lists only the newest.

2. Read the severity counts

Read the counts from the check run's output.text field, which holds the Details text. Replace CHECK_RUN_ID with the ID:

bash theme={null} gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/check-runs/CHECK_RUN_ID --jq ' (.output.text | split("\n") | last | scan("^<!-- bughunter-severity: (.*) -->$")[0] | fromjson)? // error("no severity line")'

This prints a JSON object with a count per severity and its keys in alphabetical order, for example {"nit": 1, "normal": 2, "pre_existing": 0}. Except on a check run that kept an earlier result, the counts include findings from earlier reviews of the pull request whose threads are still open.

Under the title Code review skipped — no new changes, the counts leave out nits and pre-existing findings from earlier reviews that are still open. No Important finding from the earlier review is still open then.

3. Act on the result

Have your script handle these cases in order:

  • The title starts with Code review not repeated: Code Review kept an earlier result whose Important findings are still open, and the check run has no severity line. Read the title before the counts, with gh api repos/OWNER/REPO/check-runs/CHECK_RUN_ID --jq .output.title. Fail the job if you want to gate the merge.
  • The title ends with no new changes: let the job pass without reading the counts
  • normal is above zero: fail the job if you want to gate the merge. The normal key holds the count of Important findings, so Claude found at least one bug worth fixing before merge. To print only that count, add | .normal before the closing single quote.
  • The line is missing: the command prints an error that contains no severity line instead of counts, and exits with a non-zero status. Treat that as no verdict rather than as zero findings. A check run for a review that failed, timed out, was canceled, or was superseded by a newer one has no such line, and some completed reviews have none either.

docs.title: Request a review
docs.text:
If your pull request is a draft or comes from a fork, automatic reviews skip it, so request the review with a comment command. To get a review on your pull request, do one of these:

  • Open it or mark it ready: in a repository set to Once after PR creation or After every push, a review starts when you open or reopen the pull request, or mark a draft ready for review.
  • Comment a command: post @claude review on the pull request.
  • Push a commit: a push starts a review in a repository set to After every push, or on a pull request you subscribed with @claude review always. If your pull request still adds and removes the same lines after the push, Code Review can keep the earlier result instead.
  • Click Re-run: after a review fails or times out on a pull request that isn't from a fork, run it again from the check run. On a pull request that isn't from a fork, you can also click Re-run after a push that kept the earlier result.
  • Wait for the automatic retry: a review whose session was interrupted is retried once automatically. The check run's summary says when that's happening.

docs.title: Comment commands
docs.text:
Post one of these commands as a comment on the pull request:

Command What it does When to use it @claude review Starts a single review without subscribing the PR to future pushes You want one review now, such as on a pull request in a repository set to Manual, or another review right away in the other modes @claude review always Starts a review and subscribes the PR to push-triggered reviews going forward You want subsequent pushes to start reviews, such as on a high-priority PR in a repository set to Manual @claude review once Same as @claude review: starts a single review without subscribing The same cases as @claude review @claude review stop Ends the PR's subscription to push-triggered reviews, without starting a review or canceling one that's already running. Claude replies with a comment instead of a check run. You subscribed a PR with @claude review always in a repository set to Manual or Once after PR creation, and no longer want each push to start a review @claude review off or @claude review pause Same as @claude review stop The same cases as @claude review stop

In a repository set to After every push, you can't stop reviews with a comment, because pushes there start reviews with or without a subscription. To stop pushes from starting reviews on one pull request there, convert it to a draft. When you mark it ready for review again, a review starts.

For any comment command to take effect, all of these conditions have to hold:

  • Post it as a new top-level pull request comment, not an inline comment on a diff line and not the body of a review. Editing an earlier comment doesn't count.
  • Put the whole command on one line at the start of the comment. Other text can follow it. If always or stop is misspelled or on a later line, Claude reads the comment as a plain @claude review and starts a single review. Capitalization doesn't matter.
  • You need write, maintain, or admin permission on the repository. Claude checks this with GitHub for each person who comments, and comments from bots don't start reviews.
  • The pull request must be open.

When a command that starts a review is accepted, a Claude Code Review check run appears on the pull request with the title Code review queued.... The title changes to Code review in progress... when the review starts. Claude may also react to your comment with 👀, but that reaction can appear when no review starts, so look for the check run instead.

If a review is already running on the pull request's latest commit, a new request doesn't start a second one.

[!NOTE]

Before a July 2026 update, @claude review subscribed the PR to push-triggered reviews. If you relied on that behavior, comment @claude review always instead.

docs.title: What a later review covers
docs.text:
A later review that starts on its own, such as after a push, focuses on what changed since the last review and posts fewer nits and pre-existing findings. To see whether it left findings out as a result, look in the review body for a sentence that counts them:

  • Findings on code that hasn't changed since the last review: the sentence ends "outside the scope of this re-review and not posted"
  • Nits and pre-existing findings: the sentence ends "found and not posted"

To get a review that leaves none of these out, comment @claude review. It covers the whole pull request again.

docs.title: Review drafts and pull requests from forks
docs.text:
Automatic reviews skip both of these, so request the review with a comment command:

  • Draft pull requests: a comment command runs on a draft, so you can request a review before you mark the pull request ready. Pushes to a draft don't start reviews, even after @claude review always. The subscription takes effect once you mark the pull request ready.
  • Pull requests from forks: Claude doesn't review a pull request from a fork automatically, regardless of the repository's Review runs setting. To start one, comment @claude review on the pull request. The conditions for comment commands still apply, and the write access you need is to the base repository, not the fork.

On a pull request from a fork, @claude review always works too, but doesn't subscribe the pull request to reviews on later pushes. Clicking Re-run on the check run doesn't start a review there.

docs.title: Use Code Review alongside the Claude Code GitHub Action
docs.text: If the repository also runs the Claude Code GitHub Action in interactive mode with its default @claude trigger phrase, an @claude review comment starts the Action as well. To keep the two apart, set the Action's trigger_phrase input to a different phrase.

docs.title: Set up Code Review
docs.text:
Turn on Code Review for your Claude organization: connect GitHub, install the Claude GitHub App, choose repositories, and set when reviews run

As an Owner of your Claude organization, you turn on Code Review in Admin settings > Claude Code on claude.ai. Reviews run on Anthropic infrastructure, so you don't add workflow files to your repositories.

After setup, you choose how thorough reviews are and when they run in each repository. You spend more at a higher review level and when reviews run more often. See Code Review costs.

docs.title: What you need to turn on Code Review
docs.text:
First check that your organization qualifies for Code Review. Then make sure you have this access, or someone who does:

Access Needed for Owner role in your Claude organization Every step on the admin page Owner of the GitHub organization Installing the Claude GitHub App and linking it to your Claude organization. If you aren't an owner, have one install and link the app before you start Write access to each repository you add, from the GitHub account you connect to Claude Adding the repository

docs.title: Turn on Code Review
docs.text:
1. Click the Allow code review switch

Go to the Code review section of Admin settings > Claude Code and click the Allow code review switch.

If Code Review turns on right away with no dialog, your organization already has the Claude GitHub App linked or repositories added. Go to Add more repositories, then come back for the last step.

2. Connect your GitHub account

If a Connect GitHub dialog opens, click Connect. If your organization uses GitHub Enterprise Server, select your instance in the dialog first. GitHub asks you to authorize Claude, then returns you to the admin page with the Add a repository dialog open.

If Add a repository opened straight away, your account is already connected, so go on to the next step.

3. Install the Claude GitHub App

If the repositories you want are listed in the Add a repository dialog, or you find them by searching there, go on to the next step. The dialog lists a repository only if the Claude GitHub App can access it, so if they aren't there, install the app:

  • Click Install GitHub App. When no repositories are listed, it's a button in the dialog. Otherwise, it's at the bottom of the dialog's GitHub organization filter menu. GitHub's install page opens in a new tab.
  • Pick the GitHub organization that owns the repositories.
  • Choose which repositories the app can access.
  • Approve the requested permissions. The set is broader than a review uses and is shared by other Claude features, such as GitHub Actions. See what a review can access and the full permission list.
  • When the install completes, the tab returns to Claude. If it shows a Finish connecting GitHub button, click it to link the installation to your Claude organization.
  • Go back to the admin page's tab, where the list in the dialog refreshes.

4. Choose repositories

Select the repositories you want reviewed, then click Continue. Adding a repository needs write access to it from the GitHub account you connected. You can add more repositories later.

5. Click Finish

A Code review is set up dialog follows. Click Finish to turn Code Review on. If you close the dialog any other way, your repositories stay added but Allow code review stays off, and you turn it on from the switch.

Each repository starts set to review after every push, which runs the most reviews. To run fewer, set when reviews run.

6. Verify with a test pull request

Open a test pull request in one of the repositories you added, and don't mark it as a draft. A check run named Claude Code Review appears within a few minutes. If you already set the repository to Manual (@claude review), comment @claude review on the pull request to start the first review.

If no check run appears, see No check run appears on the test pull request.

Once the review arrives, send your developers Read and request reviews on a pull request, which covers the severity levels, the comment commands, and how to respond to findings.

docs.title: Set defaults for your organization
docs.text: As an Owner, you decide how thorough reviews are and how often they run. Both are in the Code review section of Admin settings > Claude Code.

docs.title: Set the default review level
docs.text:
The review level sets how thorough each review is, and a more thorough review costs more. You set one default for the organization and can override it for individual repositories.

Level What it trades Quick A lighter pass. The fastest level, at the lowest cost Standard Balanced depth, speed, and cost. The default level Deep The most thorough pass. Takes the longest and costs the most
  • Organization default: select a level under Review level and confirm with Change level. Every repository uses it unless you give that repository its own.
  • One repository: click Edit on the repository's row, then select a Review level there. The first option, Default, follows the organization. The level saves as soon as you select it.

A new level applies to reviews that start after the change. For what else drives the cost of each review, see Code Review costs and usage.

docs.title: Set when reviews run
docs.text:
Each repository has its own Review runs setting, which decides when its pull requests get reviewed.

  • Once after PR creation: a review runs when a pull request is opened, reopened, or marked ready for review
  • After every push: a review runs on pushes to the pull request branch, catching new issues as the pull request evolves and auto-resolving threads when you fix flagged issues
  • Manual (@claude review): opening or pushing to a pull request doesn't start a review. Comment @claude review to request one, or @claude review always to also subscribe the pull request to reviews on subsequent pushes.

Manual is useful for high-traffic repositories where you want to opt specific pull requests into review, or to start reviewing pull requests only once they're ready. To compare what each option does to spend, see How often reviews run.

To change the setting, click Edit on the repository's row in the Repositories table and select a Review runs option. The choice saves as soon as you select it, and the table's Review runs column shows it shortened to Once per PR, Every push, or Manual.

  • Drafts and pull requests from forks: whichever option you choose, automatic reviews skip both
  • New repositories: a repository you add from the Add a repository dialog starts at After every push. If its GitHub organization is covered as a whole, it takes that organization row's setting instead.

docs.title: Turn tip comments on or off
docs.text:
A tip comment is a short comment Claude posts on a pull request when no review starts, saying why and what to do next. Show tips on pull requests is on by default. With it on, Claude posts a tip in each of these cases, explaining:

  • The repository is set to Manual: how to request a review with a comment
  • The pull request comes from a fork: that a maintainer can request the review
  • A bot, or someone without write access who isn't the pull request's author, comments @claude review: that no review was started, and who can request one
  • The GitHub organization isn't linked to your Claude organization: that reviews are paused, and how to link it

Turn the setting off to stop these comments.

docs.title: What developers can change
docs.text:
Developers come to you to change the review level, the Review runs setting, or which repositories get reviews. From GitHub, without the Owner role, they can do these:

  • Request a review: comment @claude review on a pull request. This needs write access to the repository, and it works on drafts and pull requests from forks, which automatic reviews skip.
  • Subscribe one pull request to a review on each push: comment @claude review always on a pull request that isn't a draft or from a fork, such as in a repository set to Manual
  • Change what reviews flag: commit REVIEW.md and CLAUDE.md files to the repository, for example to add a check

Reviews that developers request are billed to your organization. To limit what Code Review spends in a month, see Limit your spend.

docs.title: Manage repositories
docs.text: You can add repositories one at a time or cover a whole GitHub organization at once, and stop reviews wherever you don't want them.

docs.title: Add more repositories
docs.text:
To add repositories after setup, click Add above the Repositories table in the Code review section. The Add a repository dialog opens. Select repositories and click Continue.

  • A repository isn't listed: see A repository isn't listed in Add a repository.
  • You want every repository in a GitHub organization: cover the organization instead of selecting repositories one at a time

docs.title: Cover a whole GitHub organization
docs.text:
To turn on Code Review for every repository in a GitHub organization, set Review runs on the organization's row in the Repositories table. That covers every repository there that the Claude GitHub App can access, including repositories added later. This can raise spend significantly. It requires all of these:

  • The GitHub account you connected to Claude is an owner of that GitHub organization.
  • The organization is on github.com. GitHub Enterprise Server instances and personal GitHub accounts aren't eligible.
  • A monthly spend limit is set, for your Claude organization or for Code Review.

To cover the organization, click Edit on its row, select a Review runs option, and confirm. The options are the three from Set when reviews run plus Off.

After you confirm, these changes take effect:

  • Coverage: each repository is covered from its next pull request. If the Claude GitHub App was installed on selected repositories rather than all of them, Claude reviews those repositories; change the app's repository access on GitHub to cover the rest.
  • Existing settings: every repository in that GitHub organization takes the option you select, including repositories you had set individually. Setting the row again does the same. Repositories you turned off on their own rows stay off.
  • Individual changes afterward: a repository you later set differently from its organization is marked Custom in the table.
  • Review level: an organization row has no review level of its own.

docs.title: Turn off Code Review or remove a repository
docs.text:
In the Code review section of Admin settings > Claude Code, pick the control that matches what you want to stop:

  • One repository, keeping it in the list: click Edit on its row and turn off Code review. The table shows the repository as Off.
  • One repository, removing it: click Edit on its row, then Remove repository at the bottom of the dialog. Reviews stop there, and another Claude organization can then set that repository up. While the repository's GitHub organization is covered as a whole, you can't remove it; turn off its Code review switch instead.
  • A whole GitHub organization: click Edit on the organization's row and select Off. This also turns off repositories in that organization that you added one at a time.
  • Everything: turn off Allow code review. No new reviews start in any repository, and your repository list stays so you can turn it back on later.

docs.title: Troubleshoot Code Review
docs.text:
Fix a Code Review that didn't start, failed, or was skipped for budget, find missing findings, and resolve setup and REVIEW.md problems.

When Code Review doesn't do what you expect on a pull request, start with the Claude Code Review check run. Its title says how far the review got.

docs.title: Check how far the review got
docs.text:
Find the Claude Code Review check run on your pull request, then match its title to one of these common ones:

Check run title What it means What to do Code review queued... or Code review in progress... The review hasn't finished Wait for the title to change Code review found no issues The review finished and posted no findings If this isn't the pull request's first review, look in the review body for a count of findings the review left out. Otherwise, nothing A title that says issues were found The review finished with findings If you don't see them on the diff, see Find issues that aren't showing as inline comments Code review skipped — no new changes An automatic review didn't run on your latest push To get a review anyway, comment @claude review Code review not repeated — earlier findings still open An automatic review didn't run on your latest push, and Important findings from the earlier review are still open Push a fix, or to get a review anyway, comment @claude review. See When a push keeps the earlier result Code review failed or Code review timed out The review didn't finish To run it again, see Retrigger a failed or timed-out review Code review declined The review didn't run Read the check run's summary. If it names a budget or a spend limit, see Review didn't run and the PR shows a budget message No check run No review started Comment @claude review. If no check run appears after that, see A comment command didn't start a review

docs.title: A review didn't start
docs.text: Check these cases when no Claude Code Review check run appears, or when Claude posts a comment saying the review was skipped.

docs.title: A comment command didn't start a review
docs.text:
After you comment @claude review, look for a Claude Code Review check run titled Code review queued... or Code review in progress... on the pull request. An 👀 reaction on your comment doesn't confirm a review is coming. If no check run appears, check for each of these causes:

  • Code Review isn't on for this repository: Claude posts no comment and no check run in response to the command. Ask an Owner to add the repository.
  • The comment doesn't meet a condition: it was an inline comment or a review body rather than a new top-level comment, or the command wasn't at the start of the comment. Editing an earlier comment instead of posting a new one doesn't count either, and the pull request has to be open. See the conditions for comment commands and post a new comment that meets them.
  • You don't have write access: you need write, maintain, or admin permission on the repository. On a pull request from a fork, the permission that counts is on the base repository. Unless the pull request is yours, Claude can reply with a tip: "No review was started: manual reviews can only be requested by someone with write access to this repository." Ask someone with write access to comment instead.
  • The budget ran out: Claude posts a comment that begins with "⚠️ Code review skipped". See Review didn't run and the PR shows a budget message.

docs.title: Review didn't run and the PR shows a budget message
docs.text:
When your organization's budget can't cover a review, Code Review skips the review and Claude posts a comment on the pull request that begins with "⚠️ Code review skipped". In some of these cases a check run titled Code review declined also appears.

The comment links claude.ai/admin-settings/usage, where an admin restores the budget. Its wording tells you which limit was reached:

  • "has reached its monthly code review spending cap": the monthly spend limit for Code Review was reached. Reviews resume at the start of the next billing period. To get them sooner, ask an admin to raise the limit.
  • "has no extra usage available to pay for this review": your organization's usage credits balance is empty, or its overall monthly spend limit was reached. Ask an admin to add usage credits or raise that limit.
  • "is too low to start another review": what's left of the budget or balance is less than the expected cost of one review. Ask an admin to raise the limit or add usage credits.

After the budget is restored, comment @claude review on the pull request to get the review that was skipped. The conditions for comment commands apply, so the commenter needs write access.

docs.title: Retrigger a failed or timed-out review
docs.text:
If the check run's summary says "The review session was interrupted before it could finish. A new review of this commit has been queued automatically.", you don't need to do anything. That review is retried once automatically.

Otherwise, when the check run's title is Code review failed or Code review timed out, run the review again with a comment or a re-run:

  • Comment @claude review: post it as a top-level comment on the pull request. This starts a fresh review without subscribing the pull request to future pushes.
  • Click Re-run: if the pull request isn't from a fork, click Re-run on the Claude Code Review check in GitHub's Checks tab. The re-run covers the pull request's current head commit and doesn't subscribe the pull request either.

docs.title: Find issues that aren't showing as inline comments
docs.text:
If the check run title says issues were found but you don't see inline review comments on the diff, look in these other locations where findings are surfaced:

  • Check run Details: click Details next to the Claude Code Review check in the Checks tab. The severity table lists findings with their file, line, and summary regardless of whether the inline comment was accepted.
  • Files changed annotations: open the Files changed tab on the PR. A finding that has a line but wasn't posted as an inline comment appears there as an annotation on the lines concerned.
  • Review body: findings that have no inline location, or that fall outside the current diff, appear under an Additional findings heading in the review body.

docs.title: The check run mentions REVIEW.md
docs.text:
These are four of the messages a check run can carry about REVIEW.md:

  • "This review applied the repository's review instructions (REVIEW.md) from its default branch, which is not protected against direct pushes.": the review read the root file only. See Which branch REVIEW.md is read from for what protecting the branch changes.
  • "were not applied to this review: branch protection could not be confirmed": the review read no REVIEW.md.
  • "they link to a file this pull request modifies, or carry more links than the review checks": the review skipped the root REVIEW.md, or the number of subdirectory REVIEW.md files the message gives. Check the skipped file for each cause. For the root REVIEW.md, check the files it includes too:
  • Too many links: it carries more than 64 Markdown links. Cut links to 64 or fewer.
  • A link the review can't parse: it has a malformed Markdown link. Fix or remove the link.
  • A link to a changed file: it links to a file or folder this pull request changes, and the review couldn't leave out only the lines with that link. Write the rule in REVIEW.md itself.
  • "include line(s) in the root REVIEW.md were skipped on this review": your root REVIEW.md applied, but the files those lines name didn't. Check the lists under Include other files in REVIEW.md and, for a skill, under Include a skill file.

docs.title: Setup problems
docs.text: These cases come up for an Owner while setting up Code Review.

docs.title: A repository isn't listed in Add a repository
docs.text: Search for the repository by name first, because the dialog doesn't load a long list in full. The dialog lists a repository only if the Claude GitHub App can access it. Click Install GitHub App and give the app access to the repository. When no repositories are listed, Install GitHub App is a button in the dialog. Otherwise, it's at the bottom of the dialog's GitHub organization filter menu.

docs.title: No check run appears on the test pull request
docs.text: Confirm that Allow code review is on, that the repository is listed under Repositories in the Code review section, and that the Claude GitHub App has access to it. Automatic reviews skip draft pull requests, and a repository set to Manual (@claude review) needs an @claude review comment to start the first review.

docs.title: Code Review
docs.text:
Catch bugs in GitHub pull requests with Code Review: Claude reviews each change, verifies its findings, and comments inline. For Team and Enterprise plans

With Code Review, Claude reviews the pull requests in your GitHub repositories. Several agents read each change alongside the surrounding code, looking for issues such as logic errors, security vulnerabilities, or broken edge cases. A verification step checks findings against the code before they're reported.

Findings arrive as inline comments on the lines concerned, ranked by severity, with a summary and a check run on the pull request. A review never approves or blocks the pull request, so the decision to merge stays with your team.

[!NOTE]

Code Review uses AI to review code and may miss bugs, security vulnerabilities, or other issues. A review with no findings doesn't mean your code is error-free or secure.

To turn on Code Review, an Owner of your Claude organization follows Set up Code Review. Claude can also review code without this service. Run /code-review in your Claude Code session on any plan, or compare all the options.

docs.title: Availability
docs.text:
Check that your organization qualifies before you set up Code Review:

  • Plans: Team and Enterprise
  • Code hosts: repositories hosted on GitHub, including GitHub Enterprise Server and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. For data residency, have an Owner follow the GitHub Enterprise Server admin setup and enter your enterprise's ghe.com hostname.
  • Data retention: Code Review isn't available to organizations with Zero Data Retention enabled or with the HIPAA configuration applied, and isn't covered under Anthropic's Business Associate Agreement (BAA).
  • Encryption keys: Code Review isn't yet available for organizations that use customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).
  • Cloud providers: you need a Claude organization on one of these plans even if your developers use Claude Code through Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry

docs.title: Set up and use Code Review
docs.text:
Pick the page for what you need to do:

Set up Code Review

Check the requirements, install the Claude GitHub App, and choose repositories, a review level, and when reviews run

Customize Code Review

Tune what gets flagged with REVIEW.md and CLAUDE.md files in your repository

Read and request reviews on a pull request

Read the findings and their severities, and request another review with a comment

Troubleshoot Code Review

Fix a review that didn't start, failed, or was skipped for budget

Code Review costs and usage

See how reviews are billed, estimate spend, set the monthly spend limit, and track review activity

docs.title: How reviews work
docs.text:
By default, Code Review focuses on correctness: bugs that would break production, not formatting preferences or missing test coverage. To change what it flags, add guidance files to your repository.

A review runs on Anthropic infrastructure in four stages:

  1. Find: several agents examine the diff and the surrounding code in parallel.
  2. Verify: a verification step checks the candidate findings against the code and filters out false positives.
  3. Rank: the findings that remain are deduplicated and ranked by severity.
  4. Post: the review posts its results on the pull request.

Each review leaves these on the pull request:

  • Findings: inline comments on the lines concerned, with a summary in the review body
  • A check run: named Claude Code Review, with the findings listed in its details. The check run doesn't conclude as a failure.
  • A note in place of findings: posted when the check run's title reads Code review found no issues

Code Review chooses the Claude models that reviews run on, and its admin settings don't offer a model choice. To make reviews more or less thorough, change the review level.

After an Owner turns on Code Review, each repository has a setting for when reviews run: once when a pull request opens, after every push, or only on request. Whichever it is, someone with write access to the repository can comment @claude review on a pull request to start a review.

docs.title: Review levels
docs.text:
The review level sets how thorough each review is, and a more thorough review costs more:

  • Quick: a lighter pass. The fastest level, at the lowest cost.
  • Standard: balanced depth, speed, and cost. The default level.
  • Deep: the most thorough pass. Takes the longest and costs the most.

An Owner chooses one level for the organization and can give an individual repository its own, such as Quick for a routine codebase and Deep for a critical one. For what else drives the cost of each review, see Code Review costs and usage.

docs.title: What a review can access
docs.text:
A review reaches your repository through the Claude GitHub App that an Owner installs during setup:

  • Where it runs: on Anthropic infrastructure, in a managed environment. Reviews don't run in self-hosted environments.
  • What it reads and writes: inside a review, access to your repository is read-only, and a review doesn't push commits. On the pull request, it posts comments and the check run, resolves its own earlier comment threads, and can react to a comment command with 👀. The app itself holds a broader permission set that other Claude features share.
  • How it examines your code: a review works from reading the diff and the surrounding code, without building or running your code.

docs.title: Who controls a review
docs.text:
• Who can start one: where reviews run automatically, opening or pushing to a pull request starts a review, except on drafts and forks. After some pushes, Code Review keeps the earlier result instead. A comment command starts one only when it comes from a person with write access to the repository.
  • Which instructions it follows: REVIEW.md from the base or default branch and never from the pull request's own changes.

docs.title: Compare ways to get a review
docs.text:
To find the options open to you, check the Who can use it column against your plan and code host:

Option What starts a review Where it runs Who can use it Code Review Pull request activity, as each repository is set, or an @claude review comment Anthropic infrastructure Organizations on a Team or Enterprise plan with GitHub repositories, once an Owner turns it on /code-review You run the command on your branch Your Claude Code session Anyone, on any plan Ultrareview You start it from Claude Code A cloud sandbox Requires signing in with a claude.ai account. See Ultrareview for where it isn't available Claude in your own CI, with GitHub Actions or GitLab CI/CD Your pipeline's events, such as every pull request or merge request Your own CI runners Anyone with a Claude API key or cloud provider credentials, on GitHub or GitLab Your own reviewer, as a subagent or skill You or Claude invoke it during a session Wherever you run Claude Code Anyone who writes one
