docs.title: Schedule recurring tasks in Claude Code Desktop
docs.text:
Set up scheduled tasks in Claude Code Desktop to run Claude automatically on a recurring basis for daily code reviews, dependency audits, or morning briefings.

Scheduled tasks start a new session automatically at a time and frequency you choose. Use them for recurring work like daily code reviews, dependency update checks, or morning briefings that pull from your calendar and inbox.

The Desktop app's Scheduled tasks page lists both local scheduled tasks and cloud scheduled tasks, formerly routines:

  • Local task: runs on your machine with direct access to your files and tools, but only fires while the app is open and your computer is awake
  • Cloud task: runs even when your computer is off, and can also start on API calls or GitHub events

This page covers local scheduled tasks; for cloud scheduled tasks and their trigger options, see Automate work with scheduled tasks.

[!NOTE]

If your app shows the feature under its earlier name, click Routines wherever this page says Scheduled and New routine where it says New task.

docs.title: Compare scheduling options
docs.text:
Claude Code offers three ways to schedule recurring or one-off work:

Cloud Desktop /loop Runs on Cloud, Anthropic-managed by default Your machine Your machine Requires machine on No Yes Yes Requires open session No No Yes Persistent across restarts Yes Yes Restored on --resume, with exceptions Access to local files No (fresh clone) Yes Yes MCP servers Connectors configured per task Config files and connectors Inherits from session Permission prompts Auto mode by default Configurable per task Inherits from session Customizable schedule Yes Yes Yes Minimum interval 1 hour 1 minute when Claude sets it, 1 hour in the forms 1 minute

[!TIP]

Use cloud tasks for work that should run reliably without your machine. Use Desktop tasks when you need access to local files and tools. Use /loop for quick polling during a session.

[!NOTE]

By default, local scheduled tasks run against whatever state your working directory is in, including uncommitted changes. To give each run its own isolated Git worktree instead, select Worktree in the task's Edit form after you create it. The checkbox is available when the task's folder is a Git repository.

docs.title: Create a scheduled task
docs.text:
Local scheduled tasks require Claude Desktop 1.1.5368 or later.

1. Open the Scheduled tasks page

In the Code tab, click Scheduled in the sidebar or in the sidebar's More menu. If the sidebar shows Routines instead of Scheduled, click Routines, then click New routine, and continue with Full-page form.

2. Start a new task

Click New task to open the New scheduled task dialog. Check for these screens before you continue:

  • If a menu opens with Create with Claude and Set up manually, select Set up manually to open the dialog.
  • If Only on this computer is at the top of the dialog, go to Dialog with Only on this computer at the top before you enter anything.
  • If a menu with Local and Cloud opens, or a full page opens in place of the dialog, go to Full-page form.

3. Name the task

Enter a name in the Name field. Desktop converts it to lowercase kebab-case and uses it as the task's folder name on disk, so the name must be unique across your tasks.

4. Write the instructions

In the box below the name, enter what Claude should do when the task runs.

5. Turn on Only on this computer

Skip past the Trigger card for now and expand Advanced settings below it. On the General tab, turn on Only on this computer. With it on, the task runs on your machine in a local folder.

If the switch is unavailable, clear the repository or the GitHub event or API trigger, because those make the task a cloud scheduled task.

6. Pick the local folder

In the Local folder row, select a folder. Create stays unavailable until you pick one.

7. Set the schedule

Back in the Trigger card, select a schedule preset.

8. Choose the permission mode and model

In the instructions box's toolbar, select a permission mode and model. If you leave them unchanged, runs use your Claude Code settings and the default model.

9. Create the task

Click Create. If you haven't trusted the folder yet, Desktop asks you to trust it at this point. The task's detail page opens.

On the detail page, click the pencil icon to open the Edit form. There you can change the Description that Desktop filled in from your instructions, select Worktree, or switch the schedule to Manual or Custom.

You can also create a task by describing what you want in any session. For example, "set up a daily code review that runs every morning at 9am" creates a recurring task. A request like "remind me at 3pm tomorrow to check the deploy" creates a one-time task that disables itself after it fires.

docs.title: Dialog with Only on this computer at the top
docs.text:
If Only on this computer is at the top of the New scheduled task dialog when it opens, turn it on before you enter anything. When you turn it on, a separate blank form for a local task replaces the form.

Then fill in the local form's fields:

  • Name: enter a name, as in the steps to create a scheduled task.
  • Description: enter a description. Create stays unavailable until you do.
  • The instructions box: enter what Claude should do when the task runs. Select the permission mode and model from the menus in the box.
  • Working folder: select the folder the task runs in. Create stays unavailable until you select one.
  • Trigger: select a schedule. For the presets, see Schedule options.

Click Create. The task's detail page opens.

docs.title: Full-page form
docs.text:
If a menu with Local and Cloud opens, select Local. A page titled New local routine or New local scheduled task opens. Fill in its fields:

  • Name: enter a name that is unique across your tasks.
  • Description: enter one.
  • Instructions: enter what Claude should do when the task runs. In the same box, select the permission mode, the model, and the folder the task runs in.
  • Schedule: select one of the schedule options.

If Create is unavailable, hover over it to see what the form still needs. Click Create, and the task's detail page opens.

docs.title: Schedule options
docs.text:
When you turn on Only on this computer under Advanced settings, the Trigger card offers Hourly, Daily, Weekdays, and Weekly. To get Manual or Custom for such a task, open its Edit form after you create it. That form, the dialog with Only on this computer at the top, and the full-page form offer these six options:

  • Hourly: runs every hour
  • Daily: runs every day at the local time you pick
  • Weekdays: same as Daily but skips Saturday and Sunday
  • Weekly: shows a time picker and a day picker
  • Manual: no schedule, only runs when you click Run now. Useful for saving a prompt you trigger on demand
  • Custom: runs on a cron expression that you enter and that is evaluated in your local time, such as 0 9 * * * for 9:00 AM each day. Write days of the week and months as numbers, since their names aren't accepted. Sunday is 0, not 7. The form rejects an expression that runs more often than once per hour.

You can also ask Claude in any Desktop session to set the schedule. Claude isn't held to the once-per-hour limit and can set a single run at a future time. For example, ask "run the test suite every 30 minutes" or "next Monday at 9am, summarize the pull requests merged since Friday."

docs.title: How scheduled tasks run
docs.text:
Local scheduled tasks run on your machine. Desktop checks the schedule every minute while the app is open and starts a fresh session when a task is due, independent of any manual sessions you have open. Each task gets a small delay of a few minutes after the scheduled time to stagger API traffic. The delay is deterministic: the same task always starts at the same offset.

Tasks only run while the desktop app is running and your computer is awake. If your computer sleeps through a scheduled time, the run is skipped. To prevent idle-sleep, turn on Keep computer awake in Settings > This computer > System. Closing the laptop lid still puts it to sleep.

[!NOTE]

For tasks that need to run even when your computer is off, or that should trigger on an API call or GitHub event, create a cloud scheduled task instead.

docs.title: Find a run's session
docs.text:
To open the session a run started, go to the task's detail page and click that run's row in the History list.

The sidebar's session list can show a Scheduled group as well, with one row per task. To open the session of a task's latest run, click the task's row in that group. To show the group, check which layout you have:

  • Current layout: open the Group and sort menu, select Show, then select Scheduled. The group starts collapsed, so click its heading to expand it. Show lists Scheduled when at least one of your tasks is Active, the Status a task's detail page shows. If it isn't listed, use the History list, which works whether or not the group shows.
  • Earlier layout: the group is in the session list with nothing to turn on

In a run's session, whichever way you reached it, you can see what Claude did, review changes, and respond to permission prompts. Claude can edit files, run commands, create commits, and open pull requests, the same as in a session you start yourself.

docs.title: Missed runs
docs.text:
When the app starts or your computer wakes, Desktop checks whether each task missed any runs in the last seven days. If it did, Desktop starts exactly one catch-up run for the most recently missed time and discards anything older. A daily task that missed six days runs once on wake. Desktop shows a notification when a catch-up run starts.

Keep this in mind when writing prompts. A task scheduled for 9am might run at 11pm if your computer was asleep all day. If timing matters, add guardrails to the prompt itself, for example: "Only review today's commits. If it's after 5pm, skip the review and post a summary of what was missed."

docs.title: Permissions for scheduled tasks
docs.text:
Each task has its own permission mode, which you set when creating or editing the task. Allow rules from ~/.claude/settings.json also apply to scheduled task sessions. If a task runs in Manual mode and needs to run a tool it doesn't have permission for, the run stalls until you approve it. To approve it, find the run's session and answer the permission prompt there.

To avoid stalls, click Run now after creating a task, watch for permission prompts, and select "always allow" for each one. Future runs of that task auto-approve the same tools without prompting. You can review and revoke these approvals from the task's detail page.

MCP tools marked requiresUserInteraction prompt on every call and don't offer an always-allow option. Runs that call these tools stall each time.

docs.title: Manage scheduled tasks
docs.text:
In the Code tab, click Scheduled in the sidebar, then click a task in the list to open its detail page. From here you can:

  • Run now: start the task immediately without waiting for the next scheduled time
  • Status: toggle between Active and Paused to pause or resume scheduled runs without deleting the task
  • Edit: change the instructions, schedule, folder, or other settings
  • Review history: see every past run, including skipped runs. Hover a skipped entry to see why: your computer was asleep, the previous run was still in progress, or other scheduled tasks were already running. Click Show more to load older entries.
  • Review allowed permissions: see and revoke saved tool approvals for this task from the Always allowed panel
  • Delete: remove the task. The sessions the task created are archived, not deleted. The folder holding the task's SKILL.md file stays on disk at ~/.claude/scheduled-tasks/<task-name>/, or at scheduled-tasks/<task-name>/ under CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR if you set that variable. To remove that folder, delete it yourself.

You can also list, create, edit, and pause tasks by asking Claude in any Desktop session. For example, "pause my dependency-audit task" or "show me my scheduled tasks." To delete a task, use the Delete button on its detail page.

A scheduled task can also modify its own schedule or prompt from within a running session using the update_scheduled_task MCP tool. This lets a task reschedule itself based on what it finds, for example, rescheduling a code review to run earlier when it detects a release branch has been created.

To edit a task's prompt on disk, open ~/.claude/scheduled-tasks/<task-name>/SKILL.md (or under CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR if set). The file uses YAML frontmatter for name and description, with the prompt as the body. Changes take effect on the next run. Schedule, folder, model, and enabled state are not in this file: change them through the Edit form or ask Claude.

docs.title: Related resources
docs.text:
• Cloud scheduled tasks: run tasks in the cloud on a schedule, via API call, or in response to GitHub events, even when your computer is off
  • Run prompts on a schedule: session-scoped scheduling with /loop in the CLI
  • Claude Code GitHub Actions: run Claude on a schedule in CI instead of on your machine
  • Use Claude Code Desktop: the full Desktop app guide

docs.title: Claude Code Desktop in WSL
docs.text:
Run Code sessions inside a WSL 2 distribution on Windows

On Windows, the Code tab can run a session inside a WSL 2 distribution instead of on Windows itself. The session's Claude Code process, its tools, and git all execute inside the distribution, using its Linux toolchain and native Linux paths, the same environment your project targets.

Use a WSL session when your repository lives inside the distribution's filesystem. Working on those files from Windows goes through a network filesystem, which is slow and breaks file watching; running the session inside the distribution avoids both.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• Windows 10 or 11 with WSL 2. WSL 1 isn't supported.
  • At least one installed distribution (for example, Ubuntu).
  • git installed inside the distribution.

docs.title: Start a WSL session
docs.text:
1. Pick a distribution

Start a new session in the Code tab and open the environment selector under the prompt box, or above it in the earlier layout. Your installed WSL 2 distributions appear under WSL. Pick one.

2. Choose a folder

The session starts in the distribution's home directory. Use the folder picker to choose a project folder. Browsing happens inside the distribution, with Linux paths like /home/you/project.

3. Trust the folder

The first session in a folder shows the workspace trust dialog. You grant trust per distribution and folder. A folder you trust in one distribution isn't trusted in another distribution or at the same path on Windows.

The first session in a distribution takes a little longer while Claude sets up inside it. You can also open a \\wsl.localhost\... folder from the normal folder picker, and it reopens inside that distribution.

docs.title: What works in a WSL session
docs.text:
Parallel sessions, side chats, visual diff review, branch and pull request status, and worktrees all work, backed by the git and toolchain inside the distribution. "Open in editor" opens VS Code connected to the distribution through Remote - WSL.

If a Desktop feature is unavailable or limited in a WSL session, check whether it's one of these:

  • Terminal and connectors: your session may lack the integrated terminal, connectors, or both. See If the terminal or connectors are unavailable.
  • Plugins: not available in WSL sessions
  • File editing: you can view files in the file pane but can't edit them there, so ask Claude to make the changes
  • Attachments: if the + menu shows Add image in place of Add files or photos, you can attach only images. See Add files and context to prompts.

docs.title: If the terminal or connectors are unavailable
docs.text:
You can't turn on the integrated terminal or connectors for a WSL session yourself:

  • Claude account: the two features are rolling out separately. Select Help > Check for Updates…, and if a feature is still missing after you update, there's nothing to do.
  • Third-party provider: WSL sessions don't get the terminal or connectors, and updating Desktop doesn't change that

docs.title: Managed devices
docs.text: On devices managed by an organization, WSL sessions may be unavailable. If session start fails with a message that the device is managed, that's controlled by your administrator. Administrators: see how settings reach devices in the deployment guide.

docs.title: Desktop application
docs.text:
Get more out of Claude Code Desktop: parallel sessions with Git isolation, drag-and-drop pane layout, integrated terminal and file editor, side chats, computer use, Dispatch sessions from your phone, visual diff review, app previews, PR monitoring, connectors, and enterprise configuration.

In the Claude Desktop app, Claude Code is the Code tab. The app also has chat and Cowork, which handles Dispatch and longer agentic work. This page is the reference for the Code tab.

Download for macOS

Universal build for Intel and Apple Silicon

Download for Windows

For x64 processors

Get Claude for Linux (beta)

apt or .deb for Ubuntu and Debian

For Windows ARM64, download the ARM64 installer. On Linux, install with apt; see Claude Desktop on Linux.

After installing, launch Claude, sign in, and click the Code tab. For a walkthrough of your first session, see the Get started guide.

In the Code tab, each conversation is a session: it has its own chat history and project folder, independent of any other session. The sidebar lists your sessions and lets you run several in parallel. Within a session you can:

  • Review and comment on diffs, then watch the resulting PR through CI
  • Preview your running app in the Browser pane while Claude verifies its own changes, and open external sites alongside it
  • Watch Claude run and test your iOS app in the iOS Simulator pane
  • Arrange panes for the chat, diff, browser, terminal, and file editor side by side
  • Ask a side question that uses the session's context without derailing it
  • Let Claude check on, message, or archive your other sessions
  • Connect external tools like GitHub, Slack, and Linear
  • Let Claude open apps and control your screen
  • Run on your machine, in the cloud, or over SSH

For scheduled recurring work, keyboard shortcuts, or sending tasks from your phone, see the linked pages and sections. If you already use the terminal-based CLI, see the CLI comparison for what carries over.

docs.title: Start a session
docs.text:
Before you send your first message, choose the environment, project folder, permission mode, and model in the row under the prompt box:

  • Environment: use the environment selector, the first control in the row, to choose where Claude runs. See environment configuration.
  • If a new session has no environment selector under the prompt box, follow the earlier layout's steps.
  • Project folder: click the project folder control, next to the environment selector, to choose the folder Claude works in.
  • Cloud session: select repositories instead of a folder
  • Saved local or SSH environment: the environment already holds its folders, so the row shows no project folder control. To change the folders, edit the environment.
  • Permission mode: use the mode selector to choose how much autonomy Claude has. You can change the permission mode during the session.
  • Model: pick a model from the model picker toward the right end of the row. You can change the model during the session.

Type your task and press Enter to start. Each session tracks its own context and changes independently.

docs.title: Work with code
docs.text: Give Claude the right context, control how much it does on its own, and review what it changed.

docs.title: Use the prompt box
docs.text:
Type what you want Claude to do and press Enter to send. Claude reads your project files, makes changes, and runs commands based on your permission mode. You can redirect Claude at any point: click the stop button to interrupt immediately, or type a correction and press Enter to send it without stopping the running action. Claude reads the correction as soon as the current action completes and adjusts before its next step.

Click the + button next to the prompt box for file attachments, skills, connectors, and plugins.

docs.title: Accept a suggested prompt
docs.text:
After Claude replies, the Code tab can show a suggested next prompt as gray text in the empty prompt box. Claude Code generates each suggestion from your conversation with a short background request that counts toward your plan's usage limits or your API costs.

  • Use the suggestion: press Tab or Right arrow to place it in the prompt box, edit it if you want, then press Enter to send it. Pressing Enter before you accept the suggestion doesn't send it.
  • Write your own prompt: start typing. The suggestion shows only while the prompt box is empty and has no attached files.

Go to Settings > Claude Code and turn off Prompt suggestions under Sessions to stop suggestions in each session from the next time it starts or resumes.

docs.title: Add files and context to prompts
docs.text:
To give Claude a file, @mention it or attach it in the prompt box:

  • @mention files: type @ followed by a filename to add a file to the conversation context.
  • In a cloud session: @ can list files only after you send your first message. If @ lists none, send your first message without the file, then @mention the file in your next message.
  • Attach files: attach images, PDFs, and other files to your prompt from the + button next to the prompt box, or drag and drop files directly into the prompt. This is useful for sharing screenshots of bugs, design mockups, or reference documents.
  • In a WSL session: if the + menu shows Add image instead of Add files or photos, you can attach only images. To give Claude any other file from the session's folder, @mention it.

docs.title: Choose a permission mode
docs.text:
Permission modes control how much autonomy Claude has during a session: whether it asks before editing files, running commands, or both. You can switch permission modes at any time using the mode selector in the row under the prompt box. To approve each change yourself, switch to Manual.

To set a default mode for new local sessions, add permissions.defaultMode to your settings file. The desktop app reads the same settings files as the CLI. A mode you pick in the selector is remembered per folder and takes precedence over defaultMode for that folder, except Plan, which applies to the current session only.

Mode Settings key Behavior Manual default Claude asks before editing files or running commands. You see a diff and can accept or reject each change. Accept edits acceptEdits Claude auto-accepts file edits and common filesystem commands like mkdir, touch, and mv, but still asks before running other terminal commands. Use this when you trust file changes and want faster iteration. Plan plan Claude reads files and runs commands to explore, then proposes a plan without editing your source code. Good for complex tasks where you want to review the approach first. Auto auto Claude runs without routine prompts; before actions such as shell commands and network requests run, a background classifier checks that they align with your request. Appears when auto mode is available; there is no separate Settings toggle for it. Bypass permissions bypassPermissions Claude runs without permission prompts, except for the actions no mode auto-approves, safety classifiers when Claude acts on external sites, or desktop actions such as deleting a session, though not archiving one. Equivalent to --dangerously-skip-permissions in the CLI. On Pro and Max plans, enable it in your Settings → Claude Code under "Allow bypass permissions mode"; on Team and Enterprise plans there is no Settings toggle, and organization policy controls it instead. Only use this in sandboxed containers or VMs.

Earlier versions of the Code tab labeled these modes Ask permissions, Auto accept edits, and Plan mode.

The dontAsk permission mode is available only in the CLI.

[!TIP]

Start complex tasks in Plan so Claude maps out an approach before making changes. Once you approve the plan, switch to Accept edits or Manual to execute it. See plan mode for more on this workflow.

Cloud sessions support Accept edits, Plan, and Auto. Accept edits corresponds to default mode: cloud sessions pre-approve file edits, so the selector shows Accept edits instead of Manual. Bypass permissions isn't available in cloud sessions, including sessions in a self-hosted environment.

Enterprise admins can restrict which permission modes are available. See enterprise configuration for details.

docs.title: Auto mode availability
docs.text:
Auto mode is available to all users on the Anthropic API and requires Claude Opus 4.6 or later, Sonnet 4.6 or later, Haiku 5.5, or a Fable model. Organization administrators can turn auto mode off with the disableAutoMode key in managed settings.

In Enterprise deployments that route Desktop to Google Cloud's Agent Platform, auto mode is also available by default; see Auto mode on Bedrock, Agent Platform, or Foundry for the supported models.

docs.title: Preview your app
docs.text:
Claude can start a dev server and open it in the Browser pane to verify its changes. This works for frontend web apps as well as backend servers: Claude can test API endpoints, view server logs, and iterate on issues it finds. In most cases, Claude starts the server automatically after editing project files. You can also ask Claude to preview at any time. By default, Claude auto-verifies changes after every edit.

In a local session, click an HTML, PDF, or video path in the chat to open it in the Browser pane.

[!NOTE]

In an SSH session, Claude can't open your app in the Browser pane, because it doesn't have the pane's tools there. To look at the app yourself, forward its port to your computer.

If the Browser pane isn't open after Claude starts a server in a local session, click Open on the server's card in the chat.

From the Browser pane, you can:

  • Interact with your running app directly in the Browser pane
  • Watch Claude verify its own changes automatically: it takes screenshots, inspects the DOM, clicks elements, fills forms, and fixes issues it finds
  • Start or stop servers, or stop them all at once, from the Dev servers menu in the Browser pane's header
  • Choose whether the Browser keeps cookies after you quit the app with Keep cookies in the Browser pane's ⋮ menu, so you don't have to sign in again during development

Claude creates the initial server configuration based on your project. If your app uses a custom dev command, edit .claude/launch.json to match your setup. See Configure preview servers for the full reference.

To clear the Browser's saved data, select Clear browsing data in the Browser pane's ⋮ menu. To turn the Browser off entirely, turn off Browser tools in Settings > Claude Code.

docs.title: Browse external sites
docs.text:
The Browser pane is a tabbed browser, so you can open documentation, issue trackers, or any other site next to your running app. To open the Browser, press Cmd+Shift+B on macOS or Ctrl+Shift+B on Windows, or click Browser in the session's title bar. You can sign in to sites in the pane, including popup sign-in flows such as Google OAuth.

The first time you click an external link in the chat, a dialog asks whether links open in the Browser pane or in your default browser. To change your choice later, use Open links in built-in browser in the Browser pane's ⋮ menu. Cmd-click on macOS or Ctrl-click on Windows opens a link in your default browser directly.

Claude can read and interact with external pages using the same tools it uses to verify your app, with two additional safety checks:

  • Safety classifiers review Claude's write actions on external pages, such as clicking and typing, in every permission mode. These are the same classifiers auto mode uses, and when they flag an action, you get a permission prompt regardless of mode.
  • In permission modes other than Auto and Bypass permissions, a domain allowlist check also applies before Claude navigates to a new site.

docs.title: Approve Claude's actions on a site
docs.text:
The first time Claude acts on an external site, a permission card appears and Claude waits for your choice: Allow once, Always allow, or Deny. Allow once approves the action without saving anything. Always allow saves the approval for that site on your device, and you can revoke it in Settings. Each site needs its own approval, including subdomains. Your local dev servers and project files don't need approval, so auto-verify keeps working without prompts.

Even on an approved site, Claude won't purchase items, create accounts, or bypass CAPTCHAs without your input. Browsing in the Browser pane uses the same safety model as the Claude in Chrome extension. See Using Claude in Chrome safely for how Claude handles sensitive sites and risky actions.

docs.title: Choose between the Browser and the Chrome extension
docs.text: The Browser pane uses a clean browser profile, separate from your personal browser, with none of your saved logins or history. Use it for building and testing your app and for sites that don't need your identity. When you want Claude to act as you in your logged-in sessions, use the Claude in Chrome extension instead, which shares your browser's login state.

docs.title: Restrict external browsing for your organization
docs.text:
The Browser follows the same site allowlist and blocklist controls as the Claude in Chrome extension. If your organization already configured those lists for the extension, the Browser respects them automatically. Administrators can also turn off Claude's tools on external pages with the browserExternalPageTools managed setting. With tools disabled, users can still visit external sites; Claude's tools can't read or act on them.

To turn off external browsing entirely, set the disableBrowserExternalNavigation managed setting to true. This blocks all external navigation in the Browser, including sites on your organization's allowlist; localhost dev servers and file previews keep working. Use browserExternalPageTools to let users keep browsing external sites without Claude's tools, and disableBrowserExternalNavigation to block external sites for both users and Claude.

docs.title: Review changes with diff view
docs.text:
After Claude makes changes to your code, the diff view lets you review modifications file by file before creating a pull request. To open the diff view, click the line counts, such as +12 -1, in the Changes card of the session details panel. You can also click Changes in the session's title bar.

To comment on specific lines, hover over a line and click the + that appears beside its line number to open a comment box. Type your feedback and press Enter to add the comment. After adding comments to multiple lines, submit all comments at once:

  • macOS: press Cmd+Enter
  • Windows: press Ctrl+Enter

Claude reads your comments and makes the requested changes, which appear as a new diff you can review.

docs.title: Review your code
docs.text:
To have Claude review your changes before you commit, enter /code-review in the prompt box. The findings arrive in the conversation when the review completes.

In local, SSH, and WSL sessions, the findings appear as a Code review card, grouped by file. Use the card to act on them:

  • Click Walk through in diff to open the diff view and step through the findings one at a time. A finding in the current diff appears at its line, where you can click Fix this one or dismiss it.
  • Click Apply fixes to ask Claude to fix the findings that are still open.

In any session, you can also ask Claude in the prompt box to fix what the review found. For what /code-review looks for and the arguments it takes, see Review locally with /code-review.

docs.title: Monitor pull request status
docs.text:
To have Claude fix failing checks, or to have GitHub merge the pull request, turn on Auto-fix or Merge when ready. After you open a pull request, it appears in the Changes card of the session details panel with the status of its CI checks. Open the ⋮ menu beside its title:

  • Auto-fix: in a local session, Claude also addresses new review comments that someone other than you leaves. The comment's author has to be the repository's owner, an organization member, a collaborator, or a GitHub App.
  • Merge when ready: turns on GitHub's auto-merge for the PR. In a local session, Desktop requests a squash merge unless the base branch uses a merge queue.
  • In SSH and WSL sessions: Merge when ready is disabled, so turn on auto-merge for the pull request on GitHub
  • If the repository doesn't allow auto-merge: Merge when ready doesn't turn on, so enable auto-merge in your GitHub repository settings first
  • Earlier layout: once the session has a pull request, click CI on its status bar.

To archive the session automatically once the PR merges or closes, turn on auto-archive in Settings > Claude Code.

[!NOTE]

PR monitoring requires the GitHub CLI (gh) to be installed and authenticated on your machine. If gh is not installed, Desktop prompts you to install it the first time you try to create a PR.

In an SSH session, set up git and gh on the remote machine before you click Create PR, because Claude pushes the branch and runs gh pr create there. Install gh there yourself, because Desktop doesn't prompt you to in an SSH session. Then check there that git push works and that gh auth status reports that you are logged in.

docs.title: Arrange your workspace
docs.text:
The Code tab is built around panes you can arrange in any layout: chat, diff, browser, terminal, file, plan, tasks, and subagent, along with the iOS Simulator on macOS. Drag a pane by its header to reposition it, or drag a pane edge to resize it. Press Cmd+\ on macOS or Ctrl+\ on Windows to close the focused pane.

To open another pane, click its icon button in the session's title bar. Hover to see each button's name, such as Terminal, Changes for the diff view, Browser, and Files. If the pane you want has no button in the title bar, select it from the ⋮ menu beside the buttons:

  • When the window is narrow: buttons that don't fit move into the menu
  • For panes with no button: panes such as Background tasks and Plan are listed once the session has something to show in those panes

To work across screens, pop a pane such as the diff or terminal out into its own window, and dock it back when you're done. Claude keeps working in the main window.

[!NOTE]

The pane layout, terminal, file editor, and view modes in this section require Claude Desktop v1.2581.0 or later. Open Claude > Check for Updates… on macOS or Help > Check for Updates… on Windows to update.

docs.title: See session details
docs.text: The session details panel is a set of cards beside the chat that show where the session runs, what it changed, what it's running, and its context usage. The panel appears after you start a session, while the chat is wide enough for it.

docs.title: Hide or show the session details panel
docs.text: To hide or show the panel, click Hide session rail or Show session rail in the session's title bar, or in the bar's ⋮ menu. If you still don't see the panel, check which Code tab layout you have.

docs.title: Run commands in the terminal
docs.text:
The integrated terminal lets you run commands alongside your session without switching to another app. Click Terminal in the session's title bar or press Ctrl+` on macOS or Windows. The terminal opens in your session's working directory and shares the same environment as Claude, so commands like npm test or git status see the same files Claude is editing. To open a second terminal tab, click + in the terminal pane header or right-click a folder in the chat to choose Open in terminal.

If a WSL session has no terminal, see If the terminal or connectors are unavailable. The terminal is available in local and SSH sessions, with a limit on Windows remote machines.

docs.title: Open and edit files
docs.text:
To open a file Claude mentions, click its path in the chat.

To edit a file yourself, use the file pane:

  • Local sessions: you can edit files inside the session's working directory, except some view-only ones such as .mcp.json and .claude/settings.json. To change one, open it in another app.
  • Cloud, SSH, and WSL sessions: the file pane is view-only, so ask Claude to make edits.

docs.title: Save edits in the file pane
docs.text:
By default, your edits in the file pane save on their own, so the pane shows no Save button. To save your edits yourself, uncheck Auto save in the pane's ⋮ menu. With Auto save off, click Save after you change a file to write your edits, or Cancel to revert them.

If the pane warns that the file changed on disk, click Override to write your edits over the version on disk, or Discard to drop your edits.

docs.title: Open files in other apps
docs.text:
Right-click any file path in the chat, diff viewer, or file pane to open a context menu:

  • Attach as context: add the file to your next prompt
  • Open in: open the file in an installed editor such as VS Code, Cursor, or Zed
  • Show in Finder on macOS, Show in Explorer on Windows: open the containing folder
  • Copy: a submenu that copies the file's Absolute path, Relative path, or Filename

docs.title: Switch view modes
docs.text:
View modes control how much detail appears in the chat transcript. To switch view modes, open the session menu from the caret beside the session title and select Transcript view, or press Ctrl+O on macOS or Windows to cycle through them. The Thinking mode appears in the menu only after Claude has produced thinking in the session you're viewing.

Mode What it shows Normal Tool calls collapsed into summaries, with full text responses Thinking Tool calls collapsed into summaries, plus Claude's thinking Verbose Every tool call, file read, and intermediate step Claude takes, plus Claude's thinking

Use Thinking to follow Claude's reasoning with tool calls still collapsed. Use Verbose when debugging why Claude took a particular action. Claude Desktop versions before 1.46388.1 also list a Summary mode, and a session still set to Summary opens in Normal once you update.

docs.title: Keyboard shortcuts
docs.text:
Press Cmd+/ on macOS or Ctrl+/ on Windows to see all shortcuts available in the Code tab. The table in this section shows the macOS keys. On Windows and Linux, change these keys:

  • Cmd+Option: press Alt
  • Cmd+Ctrl: press Ctrl+Alt
  • Cmd: press Ctrl

Shortcuts that start with Ctrl stay the same on every platform.

Shortcut Action Cmd / Show keyboard shortcuts Cmd N New session Cmd Option 1–9 On the new session screen in the current layout, select an environment Cmd Option 0 On the new session screen in the current layout, open the New environment dialog Cmd W Close session Ctrl Tab / Ctrl Shift Tab Switch between sessions Cmd Shift ] / Cmd Shift [ Next or previous session Esc Stop Claude's response Tab / Right arrow Accept the suggested prompt in an empty prompt box Cmd Shift D Toggle diff pane Cmd Shift B Toggle Browser pane Cmd Shift S Select an element in the Browser Ctrl ` Toggle terminal pane Cmd \ Close focused pane Cmd Ctrl W Take focused session out of split view Cmd ; Open side chat Ctrl O Cycle view modes Cmd Shift M Open permission mode menu Cmd Shift I Open model menu Cmd Shift E Open effort menu 1–9 Select item in an open menu

These shortcuts apply to the Code tab. In Desktop, Shift+Tab doesn't cycle permission modes as it does in the terminal's interactive mode.

docs.title: Check usage
docs.text:
To see how full this session's context window is, find your Code tab layout:

  • Current layout: the header of the Context card in the session details panel shows it as a percentage. Open the card to see what is using the window by category.
  • Earlier layout: click the usage ring next to the model picker. Its popover shows your context window usage.

In either layout, type /context in the prompt box to print a per-category breakdown of this session's context window in the chat.

Both layouts have the usage ring next to the model picker. Click it to see your plan usage, which is shared across all your Claude Code surfaces.

docs.title: Let Claude use your computer
docs.text:
Computer use lets Claude open your apps, control your screen, and work directly on your machine the way you would. Ask Claude to interact with a desktop tool that has no CLI, or automate something that only works through a GUI. For running and testing iOS apps, Desktop opens the dedicated iOS Simulator pane instead of controlling your screen; the pane works without enabling computer use.

[!NOTE]

Computer use is a research preview on macOS and Windows that requires a Pro or Max plan. It is not available on Team or Enterprise plans. The Claude Desktop app must be running. On macOS, computer use requires macOS 14 or later.

Computer use is off by default. Enable it in Settings before Claude can control your screen. On macOS, you also need to grant Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions.

On macOS, computer use can also run in the background: Claude works in the apps you've approved while you keep working.

[!WARNING]

Unlike the sandboxed Bash tool, computer use runs on your actual desktop with access to whatever you approve. Claude checks each action and flags potential prompt injection from on-screen content, but the trust boundary is different. See the computer use safety guide for best practices.

docs.title: When computer use applies
docs.text:
Claude has several ways to interact with an app or service, and computer use is the broadest and slowest. It tries the most precise tool first:

  • If you have a connector for a service, Claude uses the connector.
  • If the task is a shell command, Claude uses Bash.
  • If the task is browser work and you have Claude in Chrome set up, Claude uses that.
  • If the task is running or testing an iOS app, Claude uses the iOS Simulator pane, which doesn't use screen control.
  • If none of those apply, Claude uses computer use.

The per-app access tiers reinforce this: browsers are capped at view-only, and terminals and IDEs at click-only, steering Claude toward the dedicated tool even when computer use is active. Screen control is reserved for things nothing else can reach, like native apps, hardware control panels, or proprietary tools without an API.

docs.title: Enable computer use
docs.text:
Computer use is off by default. If you ask Claude to do something that needs it while it's off, Claude tells you it could do the task if you enable computer use in Settings.

1. Update the desktop app

Make sure you have the latest version of Claude Desktop. On macOS and Windows, download or update at claude.com/download; on Linux, update through your package manager (instructions). Then restart the app.

2. Turn on the toggle

In the desktop app, go to Settings > This computer > System. Under Computer use, turn on Enable computer use. On Windows, the toggle takes effect immediately and setup is complete. On macOS, continue to the next step.

If you don't see the toggle, confirm you're on macOS or Windows with a Pro or Max plan, then update and restart the app.

3. Grant macOS permissions

On macOS, grant two system permissions before the toggle takes effect:

  • Accessibility: lets Claude click, type, and scroll
  • Screen Recording: lets Claude see what's on your screen

The Settings page shows the current status of each permission. If either is denied, click the badge to open the relevant System Settings pane.

docs.title: App permissions
docs.text:
The first time Claude needs to use an app, a prompt appears in your session. Click Allow for this session or Deny. Approvals last for the current session, or 30 minutes in Dispatch-spawned sessions.

The prompt also shows what level of control Claude gets for that app. These tiers are fixed by app category and can't be changed:

Tier What Claude can do Applies to View only See the app in screenshots Browsers, trading platforms Click only Click and scroll, but not type or use keyboard shortcuts Terminals, IDEs Full control Click, type, drag, and use keyboard shortcuts Everything else

Apps with broad reach, like terminals, Finder or File Explorer, and System Settings or Settings, show an extra warning in the prompt so you know what approving them grants.

The Computer use section in Settings > This computer > System includes these options:

  • Denied apps: add apps here to reject them without prompting. Claude may still affect a denied app indirectly through actions in an allowed app, but it can't interact with the denied app directly.
  • Unhide apps when Claude finishes: when computer use isn't running in the background, Claude hides your other windows while it works so it interacts with only the approved app. When Claude finishes, hidden windows are restored unless you turn this setting off.

docs.title: Manage sessions
docs.text: Each session is an independent conversation with its own context and changes. You can run multiple sessions in parallel, branch off side chats, let Claude check on and message your other sessions, send work to the cloud, or let Dispatch start sessions for you from your phone.

docs.title: Work in parallel with sessions
docs.text:
Click + New in the sidebar, or press Cmd+N on macOS or Ctrl+N on Windows, to work on multiple tasks in parallel. Press Ctrl+Tab and Ctrl+Shift+Tab to switch between sessions.

You can also open a second session next to the current session or in a window of its own:

  • Side by side: hold Option on macOS or Alt on Windows and click a session in the sidebar, or right-click the session and select Open in, then Split view
  • In its own window: hold Cmd on macOS or Ctrl on Windows and click a session, or right-click the session and select Open in, then New window

In the split view, the pane you opened or clicked last has focus, and the other pane is dimmed. To change which session a pane shows, click in that pane to give it focus, then click a session in the sidebar. To take the focused session out of the split view, press Cmd+Ctrl+W on macOS or Ctrl+Alt+W on Windows.

docs.title: Run a session in its own worktree
docs.text:
In a project that's a Git repository, turn on Worktree before you start a session to run it in its own Git worktree, an isolated copy of the project. By default, Worktree is off and Claude works in the project folder itself. On the current layout, turn on the Worktree button in the row under the prompt box.

  • With a third-party provider: if the row under the prompt box shows the project folder control but no Worktree button, click that control and turn on Worktree
  • As the default for a saved local or SSH environment: set Worktree when you create or edit the environment
  • Earlier layout: select the worktree checkbox beside the branch name, above the prompt box

Worktrees are stored in <project-root>/.claude/worktrees/ by default. To store them in a custom directory instead:

  • Local sessions: set Worktree location in Settings > Claude Code
  • SSH sessions: set Worktree folder on the SSH connection

You can also set a Branch prefix in Settings > Claude Code. Desktop prepends it to every worktree branch name, which is useful for keeping Claude-created branches organized.

To include gitignored files like .env in new worktrees, create a .worktreeinclude file in your project root. See What worktrees share with the main checkout for where a worktree session reads project settings, hooks, and skills.

[!NOTE]

Session isolation requires Git. Most Macs include Git by default. Run git --version in Terminal to check; if it prints a version number, Git is installed. If you run into Git errors, ask Claude in Cowork to help troubleshoot your setup.

docs.title: Add folders to a session
docs.text:
Add folders before the session starts or while it runs:

  • Before a local session starts: add the folders under Folders when you create a saved environment or edit one, then start the session from that saved environment.
  • While a local or SSH session runs: click + next to the prompt box and select Add folder. Claude works in that folder itself, with no worktree.

docs.title: Archive a session
docs.text:
Before you archive a session whose worktree has uncommitted changes, see Keep uncommitted changes when a session is archived. To archive a session, hover over it in the sidebar, open its menu, and select Archive. The session moves to your archived sessions.

To have sessions archive themselves when their pull request merges or closes, turn on Auto-archive after PR merge or close in Settings > Claude Code. Cloud sessions and sessions that are still running don't archive themselves.

docs.title: Keep uncommitted changes when a session is archived
docs.text:
You can lose uncommitted changes in a session's worktree when the session is archived, so commit what you want to keep first:

  • If Desktop asks about the changes: select Archive anyway to discard them, or cancel and commit them
  • If the only changes are untracked files: commit the ones you want to keep before a pull request that Claude opened in the session merges, because Desktop can then delete them without asking
  • In any other case: the worktree stays on disk with its changes. For a local session, Desktop removes both about 30 days after the session is archived or you last open it, whichever is later. To keep the changes, open the session from the Archived tab and select Unarchive

docs.title: Organize and find sessions
docs.text:
You group, sort, and find sessions from an icon in the sidebar's session list:

  • Current layout: hover over a heading in the session list to show the Group and sort icon, then click it. To find archived sessions, select View all, the menu's last row, then open the Archived tab.
  • Earlier layout: the Filter icon shows without hovering. Click it to arrange the list with Group by or Sort by. To show archived sessions, select Status, then Archived.

To rename a session, open it and click the session title in the title bar.

docs.title: Check and free up context
docs.text: To check context usage, see Check usage. When context fills up, Claude automatically summarizes the conversation and continues working. You can also type /compact to trigger summarization earlier and free up context space. See the context window for details on how compaction works.

docs.title: Get notified when a session finishes
docs.text: The desktop app sends an OS notification when a Code session finishes a task and you aren't currently viewing that session. For sessions that belong to a project, you get the project's notifications instead.

docs.title: Ask a side question without derailing the session
docs.text:
A side chat lets you ask Claude a question that uses your session's context but doesn't add anything back to the main conversation. Use it when you want to understand a piece of code, check an assumption, or explore an idea without steering the session off course.

Press Cmd+; on macOS or Ctrl+; on Windows to open a side chat, or type /btw in the prompt box. The side chat can read everything in the main thread up to that point. When you're done, close the side chat and continue the main session where you left off.

Side chats are available in local, SSH, and WSL sessions. The desktop app doesn't save side chats to disk, so you can't return to one after you close the app.

docs.title: Watch background tasks
docs.text:
The tasks pane shows the background work running inside the current session: subagents, background shell commands, and dynamic workflows. Once the session has background work, open the pane with Background tasks in the title bar's ⋮ menu.

Click any entry to see its output in the subagent pane or stop it. To see what other sessions are doing, use the sidebar, or ask Claude to check on them for you.

docs.title: Work across sessions
docs.text:
Claude can list your other Code tab sessions, read what each has been doing, and send messages between them. Ask in plain language: "which session touched the auth refactor?", "what did the API session conclude?", or "tell the payments session the schema changed".

You can also ask Claude to rename or archive a session. For example, ask it to archive the sessions whose PRs have merged.

Through this surface, Claude sees only the sessions the desktop app runs itself: local, SSH, and WSL sessions in the Code tab. Claude doesn't see cloud sessions, or sessions you started from the terminal CLI or the VS Code extension, even in worktrees of the same project, so with nine terminal worktrees open and two desktop sessions, Claude answering in one of them reports the one other desktop session. Claude never lists the session you're asking from. By default it sees the 20 most recently active sessions and skips archived sessions unless you ask for them. Cross-session messaging separately lets Claude message your other Claude Code sessions, including terminal sessions.

When Claude messages another session through this surface, Claude Code shows it there as a card labeled with the sending session's title and a link back, so you can always tell where a message came from. If the receiving session is mid-task, Claude Code holds the message and Claude reads it once the current work finishes. The receiving Claude can reply, and Claude Code delivers the reply back through this surface. Claude can't deliver to an archived session, and tells you when a message doesn't go through.

Claude Code applies three safety behaviors across sessions:

  • You get an approval card before Claude archives a session, except in Auto mode and Bypass permissions mode, where Claude can archive a session without one. To be asked, switch to Manual.
  • Claude Code checks each message from this surface against the receiving session's inbound controls, even when the receiving session doesn't have cross-session messaging itself. If you set crossSessionInbound to refuse in the receiving session, Claude Code drops messages from this surface. Claude Code reports the refusal to the Claude desktop app. Before v2.1.234, Claude Code dropped every message from this surface to a receiving session without cross-session messaging.
  • Claude Code quotes each incoming message and attributes it to the session that sent it, and Claude still follows the receiving session's own permission settings when acting on one.

docs.title: Start a task that Claude suggests
docs.text:
When Claude notices something worth fixing outside your current task, it suggests that work as a task. In local and SSH sessions on the current layout, the suggestion is a card in the chat, and its buttons either start the task or keep it in this session:

  • Start: starts the task in another session. By default the task runs in the current session's environment. The card then shows the started session's state, and the sidebar lists the started session under the current session.
  • Do it here: sends the task to the current session as a message
  • Options: review or change settings such as the environment, model, worktree, and permissions before you click Start
  • Start all: when the card lists several tasks, starts each task in its own session without waiting for one task to finish before starting the next

In cloud sessions, and in local and SSH sessions on the earlier layout, the suggestion is a Suggested task card. To start the task where the card's main button says, for example Send to cloud or Start with worktree, click that button. Click the caret beside the main button for other ways to start the task, including Do it here.

docs.title: Run long-running tasks in the cloud
docs.text:
For large refactors, test suites, migrations, or other long-running tasks, select an environment under Cloud in the environment selector when starting a session. Cloud sessions run on Anthropic-managed infrastructure by default and continue even if you close the app or shut down your computer. Check back anytime to see progress or steer Claude in a different direction. You can also monitor cloud sessions from claude.ai/code or the Claude mobile app.

Cloud sessions also support multiple repositories. Choose the repositories:

  • Current layout: in the row under the prompt box, once you select a cloud environment.
  • Earlier layout: above the prompt box. To add another repository, click + beside the selected one.

See Use Claude Code in the cloud for more on how cloud sessions work. When one body of work needs many cloud sessions, use a project: Claude starts and tracks the sessions for you from one conversation. Create a project has the steps.

[!NOTE]

A task in an SSH session can also keep going while Desktop is disconnected, but with a Claude account it can stop when its sign-in expires.

docs.title: Continue in another surface
docs.text:
To continue a session somewhere else, open the session menu from the caret beside the session title or from the session's row in the sidebar, then select Open in:

  • Select Cloud to continue the session as a cloud session, with your conversation carried over as a summary. Before you confirm, the dialog states whether your files move too and whether this session is archived once the cloud one is ready. You can't move a session that runs over SSH or in WSL this way.
  • Select an installed editor or your file manager to open the session's folder on disk there.

docs.title: Control which sessions appear on your other devices
docs.text:
A local session shows up on your other devices once Remote Control connects it. A connected session appears in the session list at claude.ai/code and in the Claude apps on devices signed in to your claude.ai account.

A local session connects when you turn Remote Control on for it, or when it connects automatically as it starts:

  • You turn it on for that session: with the session's Remote Control switch, or by typing /remote-control in its prompt box.
  • It connects when it starts: new sessions connect automatically while Connect new sessions to Remote Control is on in Settings > Claude Code. If you've never changed that setting, Desktop follows remoteControlAtStartup in your user or managed settings, then your organization's default.

To see whether a session is connected, check the Remote Control switch in the Environment card of its session details panel.

To keep sessions off your other devices, turn Remote Control off at the level you need:

  • One session: turn off its Remote Control switch. In a session that connected when it started, typing /remote-control leaves Remote Control on and shows Remote Control is already on. This session connected automatically when it started. Click Turn off on that line to disconnect.
  • New Desktop sessions on this computer: turn off Connect new sessions to Remote Control in Settings > Claude Code. If it already shows off, turn it on and then off so Desktop saves your choice. Once saved, it takes precedence over remoteControlAtStartup and the defaults.
  • Any session on this computer, including the CLI: set disableRemoteControl to true in ~/.claude/settings.json to stop sessions from connecting. A session that was already connected when you saved the file stays connected until you turn Remote Control off for it.

To hide a session that already appears on your other devices, archive it in Desktop. Desktop archives the session's Remote Control copy too, so it leaves the default session list on those devices. To view or delete it there, see Archive sessions.

docs.title: Sessions from Dispatch
docs.text:
Dispatch is a persistent conversation with Claude that lives in Cowork. You message Dispatch a task, and it decides how to handle it.

A task can end up as a Code session in two ways: you ask for one directly, such as "open a Claude Code session and fix the login bug", or Dispatch decides the task is development work and spawns one on its own. Tasks that typically route to Code include fixing bugs, updating dependencies, running tests, or opening pull requests. Research, document editing, and spreadsheet work stay in Cowork.

docs.title: Follow a session that Dispatch started
docs.text:
The session that Dispatch starts appears in the Code tab's sidebar with your other sessions. With the sidebar's default grouping and sorting, look for the newest session in the group for the folder it runs in. You get a push notification on your phone when it finishes or needs your approval.

If you have computer use enabled, Dispatch-spawned Code sessions can use it too. App approvals in those sessions expire after 30 minutes and re-prompt, rather than lasting the full session like regular Code sessions.

docs.title: Set up Dispatch
docs.text:
For setup, pairing, and Dispatch settings, see the Dispatch help article. Dispatch requires a Pro or Max plan and is not available on Team or Enterprise plans.

Dispatch is one of several ways to work with Claude when you're away from your terminal. For a comparison with the other options, see Platforms and integrations.

docs.title: Extend Claude Code
docs.text:
Connect external services, add reusable workflows, customize Claude's behavior, and configure preview servers. To manage connectors, skills, and plugins in one place, click Customize in the sidebar. Cowork in the Desktop app sources its skills, plugins, and connectors from this Customize configuration, which syncs through your claude.ai account, not from the CLI's ~/.claude directory.

Claude Code also loads the skills and plugins enabled for your claude.ai account in terminal sessions where you sign in with the same account. See Skills synced from claude.ai and Plugins synced from claude.ai.

docs.title: Connect external tools
docs.text:
Connectors are MCP servers with a graphical setup flow.

Click + next to the prompt box, before or during the session, to add connectors in a local or SSH session with a Claude account. Select Add connectors to open the connector directory. If the menu shows Connectors instead, select it, then Browse connectors.

[!NOTE]

These cases are covered on other pages:

  • Connectors is grayed out in a WSL session: see If the terminal or connectors are unavailable
  • Cloud sessions: see How connectors reach Claude Code

Once connected, Claude can read your calendar, send messages, create issues, and interact with your tools directly. You can ask Claude what connectors are configured in your session. To manage or disconnect connectors, go to Settings > Connectors in the desktop app.

For integrations not listed in Connectors, add MCP servers manually via settings files. You can also create custom connectors.

docs.title: Use skills
docs.text:
Skills extend what Claude can do. Claude loads them automatically when relevant, or you can invoke one directly: type / in the prompt box or click the + button and select Slash commands to browse what's available. This includes built-in commands, your custom skills, project skills from your codebase, and skills from any installed plugins. Select one and it appears highlighted in the input field. Type your task after it and send as usual.

You can send a command while Claude is working, the same as any other message, and the session returns to idle once the turn finishes.

Local sessions load your personal skills from ~/.claude/skills/. An SSH session reads ~/.claude/skills/ from the remote host's home directory, not from your machine.

Local and cloud sessions also load the skills enabled for your claude.ai account, except local sessions when your organization sets disableSideloadFlags. Cloud sessions load them instead of ~/.claude/skills/, as Skills in Cowork and cloud sessions describes.

docs.title: Install plugins
docs.text:
Plugins are reusable packages that add skills, agents, hooks, MCP servers, and LSP configurations to Claude Code. You can install plugins from the desktop app without using the terminal.

In a local session or an SSH session, click + next to the prompt box and select Add plugins to open the plugin browser. If the menu shows Plugins instead, select it, then Browse plugins, or Manage plugins to enable, disable, or uninstall plugins.

You can scope plugins to your user account, a specific project, or local-only. If your organization manages plugins centrally, those plugins are available in desktop sessions the same way they are in the CLI, except the ones the desktop app withholds under disableSideloadFlags.

The plugin browser is not available in cloud sessions, and plugins you install from the desktop app aren't available for cloud sessions. A cloud session also doesn't install plugins that the repository's .claude/settings.json declares, as What carries over from your setup explains. Plugins aren't available in WSL sessions. For the full plugin reference including creating your own plugins, see plugins.

docs.title: Configure preview servers
docs.text:
Claude automatically detects your dev server setup and stores the configuration in .claude/launch.json at the root of the folder you selected when starting the session. Preview uses this folder as its working directory, so if you selected a parent folder, subfolders with their own dev servers won't be detected automatically. To work with a subfolder's server, either start a session in that folder directly or add a configuration manually.

To customize how your server starts, for example to use yarn dev instead of npm run dev or to change the port, edit .claude/launch.json. The file supports JSON with comments.

```json theme={null} { "version": "0.0.1", "configurations": [ { "name": "my-app", "runtimeExecutable": "npm", "runtimeArgs": ["run", "dev"], "port": 3000 } ] } 

You can define multiple configurations to run different servers from the same project, such as a frontend and an API. See the [examples](#examples) below.

#### Auto-verify changes

When `autoVerify` is enabled, Claude automatically verifies code changes after editing files. It takes screenshots, checks for errors, and confirms changes work before completing its response.

Auto-verify is on by default. Disable it per-project by adding `"autoVerify": false` to `.claude/launch.json`, or turn off **Auto-verify changes** in the Browser pane's **⋮** menu.

```json theme={null}
{
  "version": "0.0.1",
  "autoVerify": false,
  "configurations": [
    {
      "name": "my-app",
      "runtimeExecutable": "npm",
      "runtimeArgs": ["run", "dev"],
      "port": 3000
    }
  ]
}

When disabled, preview tools are still available and you can ask Claude to verify at any time. Auto-verify makes it automatic after every edit.

docs.title: Configuration fields
docs.text:
Each entry in the configurations array accepts the following fields:

Field Type Description name string A unique identifier for this server runtimeExecutable string The command to run, such as npm, yarn, or node runtimeArgs string[] Arguments passed to runtimeExecutable, such as ["run", "dev"] port number The port your server listens on. Defaults to 3000 cwd string Working directory relative to your project root. Defaults to the project root. Use ${workspaceFolder} to reference the project root explicitly env object Additional environment variables as key-value pairs, such as { "NODE_ENV": "development" }. Don't put secrets here since this file is committed to your repo. For secrets, see Set environment variables for dev servers. autoPort boolean How to handle port conflicts. See Port conflicts program string A script to run with node. See when to use program vs runtimeExecutable args string[] Arguments passed to program. Only used when program is set url string The address the preview opens instead of http://localhost:<port>. See open the preview at a specific URL

docs.title: When to use program vs runtimeExecutable
docs.text:
Use runtimeExecutable with runtimeArgs to start a dev server through a package manager. For example, "runtimeExecutable": "npm" with "runtimeArgs": ["run", "dev"] runs npm run dev.

Use program when you have a standalone script you want to run with node directly. For example, "program": "server.js" runs node server.js. Pass additional flags with args.

docs.title: Open the preview at a specific URL
docs.text:
By default, the preview opens http://localhost:<port>. Set url when your server needs a different address. Common cases are servers that require local HTTPS, apps that use *.localhost subdomains, and apps that sign you in through a redirect.

```json theme={null} { "version": "0.0.1", "configurations": [ { "name": "my-app", "runtimeExecutable": "npm", "runtimeArgs": ["run", "dev"], "port": 8443, "url": "https://localhost:8443" } ] } 

Localhost addresses open directly, exactly like the default port address. This includes `localhost`, any `*.localhost` subdomain, `127.0.0.1`, and `::1`. For security, a localhost `url` must be your server's origin alone, with no path or query. Its port must match the entry's port. To show a specific page, ask Claude to navigate there after the preview opens. A localhost `url` with a path, query, or mismatched port is reported as a configuration error that names the url and shows the fix.

For any other address, Desktop asks for your permission the first time the preview opens it, the same as when you browse to a new site in the preview. External addresses may include paths. Choose **Always allow** to skip the prompt for that site in the future. Organization policies that restrict external sites in the preview still apply.

To preview a server you already run yourself, set `url` without a command. Claude attaches the preview to your running server instead of starting one:

```json theme={null}
{
  "version": "0.0.1",
  "configurations": [
    {
      "name": "my-app",
      "url": "https://app.localhost:3000"
    }
  ]
}

The url must be http or https, and must not contain a username or password.

docs.title: Port conflicts
docs.text:
The autoPort field controls what happens when your preferred port is already in use:

  • true: Claude finds and uses a free port automatically. Suitable for most dev servers.
  • false: Claude fails with an error. Use this when your server must use a specific port, such as for OAuth callbacks or CORS allowlists.
  • Not set (default): your server gets the next free port, as with true, except in the one case below. Before Claude Desktop v2.37337.0, Claude asks whether the server needs that exact port instead, then saves your answer in launch.json.

If your preferred port is in use and autoPort is unset, your server stays stopped when all of these hold:

  • You start the server through an npm, yarn, pnpm, or bun script.
  • Your preferred port is hardcoded in that script, or Claude can't inspect the script.
  • You don't pass the port in runtimeArgs.

In that case, free the port, remove the hardcoded value, or change port to match the script. Setting "autoPort": true instead works only for a script that reads PORT.

Have your server read its port from the PORT environment variable, which carries the assigned port. When Claude moves your server to a different port, it also rewrites a --port or -p value in runtimeArgs to match.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
These configurations show common setups for different project types:

Next.js

This configuration runs a Next.js app using Yarn on port 3000:

```json theme={null} { "version": "0.0.1", "configurations": [ { "name": "web", "runtimeExecutable": "yarn", "runtimeArgs": ["dev"], "port": 3000 } ] } 

**Multiple servers**

For a monorepo with a frontend and an API server, define multiple configurations. The frontend uses `autoPort: true` so it picks a free port if 3000 is taken, while the API server requires port 8080 exactly:

```json theme={null}
{
  "version": "0.0.1",
  "configurations": [
    {
      "name": "frontend",
      "runtimeExecutable": "npm",
      "runtimeArgs": ["run", "dev"],
      "cwd": "apps/web",
      "port": 3000,
      "autoPort": true
    },
    {
      "name": "api",
      "runtimeExecutable": "npm",
      "runtimeArgs": ["run", "start"],
      "cwd": "server",
      "port": 8080,
      "env": { "NODE_ENV": "development" },
      "autoPort": false
    }
  ]
}

Node.js script

To run a Node.js script directly instead of using a package manager command, use the program field:

```json theme={null} { "version": "0.0.1", "configurations": [ { "name": "server", "program": "server.js", "args": ["--verbose"], "port": 4000 } ] } 

## Environment configuration

The environment you pick when [starting a session](#start-a-session) determines where Claude executes and how you connect:

* **Local**: runs on your machine with direct access to your files
* **Cloud**: runs on Anthropic-managed infrastructure by default. Sessions continue even if you close the app.
* **SSH**: runs on a remote machine you connect to over SSH, such as your own servers, cloud VMs, or dev containers. A running task can [keep going while Desktop is disconnected](#keep-a-task-running-while-desktop-is-disconnected), but with a Claude account it can stop when its sign-in expires.
* **WSL** (Windows): runs inside a [WSL 2 distribution](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/desktop-wsl.md) on your machine, using its Linux toolchain and native paths

### Create a saved environment

A saved environment is an entry in the [environment selector](#start-a-session) that records where Claude runs, so you can start later sessions there. A local or SSH environment also holds the folders Claude works in. Saved local and SSH environments are part of the [current layout](#check-which-layout-you-have), so if you don't see them, check which layout you have and how to get the current one.

**1. Open the New environment dialog**

Open the environment selector under the prompt box and select **New environment** at the bottom of its menu.

**2. Choose where Claude runs**

Select the **Local**, **SSH**, or [**Cloud**](#cloud-sessions) tab and fill in the form on that tab. On the **SSH** tab, choose a [connection](#ssh-sessions) and a folder on the remote machine.

**3. Save the environment**

Select **Create environment**, or **Add environment** on the **Cloud** tab.

#### Environments that Desktop creates for you

If the environment selector lists local or SSH environments you didn't create, Desktop created them for you. The first time you open the Code tab in the [current layout](#check-which-layout-you-have), Desktop creates up to eight environments. The environments come from the local and SSH folders you used most in the last month. You can [edit or delete them](#use-edit-or-remove-a-saved-environment).

#### Use, edit, or remove a saved environment

Find the environment's entry in the [environment selector](#start-a-session):

* **Start a session**: select the entry.
* **Edit or delete**: hover over the entry and click the gear icon. To delete a local or SSH environment, click **Delete environment** in **Edit environment**.
* **Archive cloud environments**: see [Archive an environment](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/cloud-environments.md#archive-an-environment).

### Environment variables in local sessions

To set an environment variable for a local session, [add it to a saved local environment](#set-environment-variables-for-local-sessions), then start a new session from that environment.

Variables such as `PATH` and `CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR` have their own instructions:

| Variable | What to do instead |
| :- | :- |
| `PATH`, the folders your system searches for programs such as `npm` | See [Session not finding installed tools](#session-not-finding-installed-tools). On Windows, Desktop doesn't read PowerShell profiles, so set `PATH` in your user or system environment variables, then quit and reopen Desktop. |
| A variable for an MCP server from [`claude_desktop_config.json`](#mcp-servers-from-the-claude-desktop-chat-app) | Quit Desktop, set it in that server's `env` block, then reopen Desktop |
| [`CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars#variables) or [`CLAUDE_CODE_TMPDIR`](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars#variables) | Set it in [one of the places you'd set a variable for dev servers](#set-environment-variables-for-dev-servers), then quit and reopen Desktop |
| `API_TIMEOUT_MS`, `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, or another variable Desktop sets itself | See [Environment variables Desktop sets itself](#environment-variables-desktop-sets-itself) |

On macOS or Linux, if a variable you set with `export` is missing or wrong in a command Claude runs, see [Exported variable missing or wrong in commands Claude runs](#exported-variable-missing-or-wrong-in-commands-claude-runs).

#### Set environment variables for local sessions

Add the variables to a saved local environment and start your sessions from it. Desktop [sets some variables itself](#environment-variables-desktop-sets-itself), such as `API_TIMEOUT_MS`, and your sessions get its value for those instead of yours.

> [!NOTE]
>
> If your environment selector is above the prompt box, you have the [earlier layout](#check-which-layout-you-have), which has no saved local environments. Use the [local environment editor](#use-the-local-environment-editor) instead.

**1. Open a local environment's form**

* **To create a saved local environment**: select [**New environment**](#create-a-saved-environment) at the bottom of the environment selector's menu, then the **Local** tab
* **To change one you already have**: in the environment selector, hover over a saved environment under **Local** and click the gear icon to open [**Edit environment**](#use-edit-or-remove-a-saved-environment)

**2. Enter the variables**

Select **Environment variables**, enter one `KEY=value` per line, and select **Done**.

**3. Save the environment**

Select **Create environment** or **Save**.

Only sessions you start from that environment get the variables.

To set a variable for every local session, add it to the [`env` key](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars#set-variables-in-settings-files) in your `~/.claude/settings.json` file. Claude Code [ignores the value](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/settings-reference.md#how-env-values-interact-with-your-shell) if that variable is already in the environment Desktop starts the session with. See [environment variables](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/env-vars.md) for the full list of supported variables.

#### Set environment variables for dev servers

To give a dev server a secret without committing it to [`launch.json`](#configure-preview-servers), set it in one of these places, then restart Desktop:

* **macOS and Linux**: export it in your shell profile
* **Windows**: add it to your user or system environment variables
* **Any platform**: save it in the [local environment editor](#use-the-local-environment-editor), if you can open it

Dev servers don't get the variables you add to a [saved environment](#create-a-saved-environment) or to `~/.claude/settings.json`.

#### Use the local environment editor

To open the local environment editor, click the gear icon on the entry for your own computer, not the one on a saved environment:

* **Selector under the prompt box**: hover over the entry for your computer, the first under **Local**. If a gear icon appears, click it. If not, the editor isn't available, so set the variable for [local sessions](#set-environment-variables-for-local-sessions) or [dev servers](#set-environment-variables-for-dev-servers) another way.
